original_question: Let P(z) be a homogeneous polynomial of degree 4 in C[z] whose Hessian matrix Hes P is nilpotent, so P is Hessian nilpotent. This is exactly the content of Conjecture 1.1 in the introduction.

justification: The draft is aiming at Conjecture 1.1 in Section 1.1, page 136, essentially verbatim. The nearby context confirms the intended notation and scope: Proposition 1.2 on page 136 gives the paper's standard criterion for Hessian nilpotency, namely that for formal power series with order at least 2, P is HN iff Delta^m(P^m)=0 for all m >= 1; this matches the role of the HN hypothesis in the conjecture. Theorem 1.3 on page 137 shows that the coefficients of the deformed inversion pair Q_t are proportional to Delta^m(P^(m+1)), explaining why the conjecture is formulated with the power m+1 rather than some neighboring exponent. If one wants a paper-explicit equivalent reformulation, Theorem 7.4 later proves that for any HN polynomial with order at least 2, the vanishing conjecture for P is equivalent to P being a polynomial in the coordinates of the associated symmetric map F=z-grad P.

original_question: Let p be a prime, let P_* be the polynomial part of the dual Steenrod algebra with P_* congruent to F_p[xi_1, xi_2, xi_3, ...], let P be its dual Hopf algebra, and consider Ext_P^{s,t}(F_p, F_p). refined_question: Let p be a prime, let P_* be the polynomial part of the dual Steenrod algebra, so that P_* is isomorphic to F_p[xi_1, xi_2, xi_3, ...], and let P denote its graded dual Hopf algebra. The Frobenius pth-power map on P_* induces an algebra endomorphism P^0: Ext_P^{s,t}(F_p, F_p) -> Ext_P^{s,pt}(F_p, F_p). Fix a homological degree s > 0. Is it true that for every internal degree t and every homogeneous class z in Ext_P^{s,t}(F_p, F_p), there exists an integer n >= 0 such that (P^0)^n(z) is nilpotent in the bigraded algebra Ext_P^{*,*}(F_p, F_p)?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, for fixed s > 0 and every t, if a homogeneous class z satisfies P^0(z) in Ext_P^{s,t}(F_p, F_p), then z is nilpotent.
justification: The draft is clearly aiming at Palmieri's Conjecture 4.1 in Section 4: the paper introduces exactly the same notation P_*, P, and P^0, and Conjecture 4.1 is stated in exactly the same eventual-nilpotence / preimage-nilpotence form. Theorem 4.2 then records that this conjecture is true for p = 2, while Conjecture 4.3 is a strictly stronger version asserting that one may always take n = 1. Because your draft asks only for eventual nilpotence under some iterate, it targets Conjecture 4.1 rather than the stronger Conjecture 4.3.

original_question: Let p = 2 and G_{2n} = GL_{2n}(F_2). target_in_paper: Section 5, Question 5.1 (Stewart Priddy): whether the determinant class det_n lies in the image of the restriction map from H^*(GL_{2n}(F_2); F_2) to H^*(A_{n,n}; F_2)^{GL_n(F_2) x GL_n(F_2)}.

refined_question: For each integer n >= 1, let G_n = GL_n(F_2) and let G_{2n} = GL_{2n}(F_2). Define the maximal elementary abelian 2-subgroup A_{n,n} = { [[I_n, U], [0, I_n]] : U in M_n(F_2) } <= G_{2n}, so that H^*(A_{n,n}; F_2) = F_2[x_{i,j} | 1 <= i,j <= n] with each x_{i,j} in cohomological degree 1. Since N_{G_{2n}}(A_{n,n}) = G_n x G_n, restriction along A_{n,n} -> G_{2n} lands in the invariant ring H^*(A_{n,n}; F_2)^{G_n x G_n}. If det_n := det(x_{i,j}) in F_2[x_{i,j}] is the resulting homogeneous invariant of degree n, is det_n in the image of the degree-n restriction map H^n(G_{2n}; F_2) -> H^n(A_{n,n}; F_2)^{G_n x G_n}?
justification: The paper states this problem explicitly in Section 5 as Question 5.1, after introducing A_{n,n}, the polynomial cohomology ring H^*(A_{n,n}; F_2), the normalizer N_{G_{2n}}(A_{n,n}) = G_n x G_n, the restriction map, and the class det_n. Your draft is therefore already aimed at the correct official problem. The main refinements needed are only to make the quantifier on n explicit, define G_n, specify the normalizer action that explains the invariant codomain, record that each x_{i,j} has degree 1, and say clearly that the question concerns the degree-n component of restriction. No alternate formulation is given because the next item in the paper, Question 5.2, is posed as a distinct stronger question, not as an explicit equivalent reformulation of Question 5.1.

refined_question: Let m > 1, and let {(t_n, sigma_n)}_{n>=1} be a stationary ergodic sequence with E sigma_1 < m E t_1. For the G/G/m queue with FCFS discipline, define the Kiefer-Wolfowitz vector of virtual waiting times by W_1 = 0 and W_{n+1} = R(W_n + e_1 sigma_n - 1 t_n)^+, where e_1 = (1,0,...,0), 1 = (1,...,1), R orders coordinates in weakly increasing order, and positive part is taken coordinatewise. It is already known that, from zero initial state, W_n converges almost surely coordinatewise to a limit with minimal stationary distribution pi_min, and hence converges weakly to pi_min. Is it true that, under these assumptions alone and without any further restriction on the driving sequence, one in fact has total-variation convergence to pi_min, namely sup_{A in B(R_+^m)} |P(W_n in A) - pi_min(A)| -> 0 as n -> infinity?
justification: This is the exact open problem in subsection 1.1. Foss first recalls the single-server G/G/1 case, where Loynes’s scheme gives total-variation convergence from any initial delay, and then turns to the multiserver G/G/m case. There he notes three points that determine the sharp formulation: multiple stationary regimes may exist in general; from x = 0 the monotone construction already yields a limit with minimal stationary distribution pi_min and therefore only weak convergence is known; and the conjecture is precisely that no additional restriction is needed to upgrade that weak convergence to total variation. Your draft is therefore very close, but it should make the Kiefer-Wolfowitz recursion explicit and identify the limiting law as pi_min rather than an arbitrary stationary distribution. original_question: For the incompressible Jeffreys-type viscoelastic fluid model on a bounded domain Ω with motion equation ∂v/∂t + Σ_i v_i ∂v/∂x_i − Div σ + ∇p = f, incompressibility condition div v = 0, no-slip boundary condition v|∂Ω = 0, and constitutive law σ + λ1 Dσ/Dt = 2η(E + λ2 DE/Dt) where E is the strain-rate tensor and D/Dt is an objective derivative, does the initial-boundary value problem admit global-in-time strong solutions for arbitrary coefficients, external force, and initial data in every spatial dimension n ≥ 2?

refined_question:
Let Ω ⊂ R^n, with n = 2 or 3, be a sufficiently smooth bounded domain. Consider the incompressible homogeneous Jeffreys/Oldroyd initial-boundary value problem with no-slip boundary condition,

u_t + (u·∇)u - Div sigma + ∇p = f_0, div u = 0, u|_{∂Ω} = 0,

sigma + lambda_1 D_a sigma/Dt = 2 eta (E(u) + lambda_2 D_a E(u)/Dt),

where 0 < lambda_2 < lambda_1, eta > 0, E(u) = (∇u + (∇u)^T)/2, and D_a/Dt is Oldroyd’s objective derivative with parameter a ∈ [-1,1]. For data in the strong-solution class used in the paper (in particular, f_0 ∈ L^2(0,T;H^1(Ω)^n) ∩ W^1_2(0,T;H^{-1}(Ω)^n), u_0 ∈ H^2(Ω)^n ∩ V, and the corresponding initial stress datum in the H^2-type symmetric-tensor class), local-in-time strong solvability is known, and global-in-time strong solvability is known only under smallness assumptions on the data and parameters. Is it true that this bounded-domain problem admits a global-in-time strong solution without any such smallness assumption, already in the case n = 2?
equivalent_formulation:
Equivalently, after setting gamma_1 = eta*lambda_2/lambda_1, mu_1 = eta - gamma_1, and tau = sigma - 2*gamma_1 E(u), one may ask for global-in-time strong solvability, without smallness assumptions, of the equivalent system

u_t + (u·∇)u - gamma_1 Δu - Div tau + ∇p = f_0,

tau + lambda_1(∂_t tau + (u·∇)tau + tau W(u) - W(u) tau - a(tau E(u) + E(u) tau)) = 2 mu_1 E(u),

div u = 0, u|_{∂Ω} = 0,

with u(0) = u_0 and tau(0) = tau_0, where W(u) = (∇u - (∇u)^T)/2.
justification: Your draft is clearly aiming at the review’s strong-solvability open problem, because it asks whether the bounded-domain incompressible Jeffreys system has global strong solutions. But in the paper-faithful formulation, the scope is narrower and sharper: the surveyed theorem gives only local strong solvability for the bounded-domain Jeffreys/Oldroyd system in dimensions 2 and 3, with Oldroyd’s derivative and specific Sobolev regularity hypotheses, while the bounded-domain global theory is only available under smallness assumptions. The unresolved point is therefore not 'arbitrary coefficients, external force, and initial data in every dimension n >= 2' in full generality, but whether one can remove the smallness assumptions and still obtain a global strong solution; the authors emphasize that this is open even in two dimensions. I therefore kept the question close to the paper’s actual intent by restricting to the exact model/scenario discussed in the strong-solution part and by phrasing the open problem at its sharpest point: global strong solvability beyond the small-data regime, already for n = 2.

justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of Beauville's Question 2. In the surrounding discussion, Beauville first recalls the K3 case, where global Torelli says that a Hodge isometry on H^2 characterizes isomorphism, then introduces the higher-dimensional period map and states that only local Torelli and surjectivity are known there. He immediately explains why the naive higher-dimensional global Torelli statement fails: any birational map induces a Hodge isometry, and Namikawa's example shows that two generalized Kummer manifolds can have the same period with appropriate markings without being bimeromorphic. He therefore asks exactly what a Hodge isometry implies for two same-dimensional hyperkähler manifolds, and whether adding further preserved structure can recover isomorphism. The next paragraph notes partial progress by Markman and Verbitsky, confirming that this is the precise nearby problem your draft is aiming at.

original_question: Is every Sylow-metacyclic finite group Q-admissible, that is, realizable as the Galois group of a maximal subfield of some crossed-product division algebra over Q?

correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's intended target very closely: it fixes the base field to Q, asks about the Sylow-metacyclic hypothesis, uses the paper's notion of Q-admissibility, and correctly paraphrases admissibility in terms of realizing the group as the Galois group of a maximal subfield of a crossed-product division algebra over Q. equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, is every finite Sylow-metacyclic group G the Galois group of a maximal subfield of some G-crossed-product Q-division algebra?
justification: The draft is aiming at §11.A, Problem 11.2, which the paper explicitly calls the Q-admissibility conjecture. The surrounding context in §11.A also explains why the Sylow-metacyclic condition is the exact one appearing in the conjecture: Schacher's theorem shows that every Q-admissible group is Sylow-metacyclic, motivating the converse problem stated as Problem 11.2. original_question: Let X be the blow-up of P^2 at r distinct points in arbitrary position, and let L be an effective nef divisor on X. u\in\{1,2,3,4\}, the set of a_
u-points of f equals the set of a_
u-points of g (and if a_
u=\infty, this means that f and g have the same pole set), and suppose moreover that for exactly one of these four shared values the multiplicities also agree, while for the other three no multiplicity agreement is assumed. Must it follow that f and g actually share all four values counting multiplicities, and hence, by Nevanlinna’s Four-Value Theorem, after a relabelling of the shared values one has (a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)=-1, two of the shared values are Picard values of both functions, and g is a Möbius transformation of f fixing the other two shared values and permuting the Picard pair? I therefore restored the missing one-CM assumption, kept the ambient setting C and \widehat{\mathbb{C}}, and retained your explicit Four-Value conclusion because that is exactly the standard consequence once one knows that all four values are shared CM. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.3383))

original_question: For a pair Theta = (theta_1, theta_2) of real numbers linearly independent together with 1, define psi_+(t) as the minimum of ||theta_1 x_1 + theta_2 x_2|| over positive integers x_1, x_2 with max(x_1, x_2) <= t, and define omega_+(Theta) by the decay rate of t^gamma psi_+(t). refined_question:
Let \Theta=(\theta_1,\theta_2)\in\mathbb R^2 be such that 1,\theta_1,\theta_2 are linearly independent over \mathbb Q, and for t\ge 1 define
\psi_+(t)=\min\{\,\|\theta_1 x_1+\theta_2 x_2\|: x_1,x_2\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ \max(x_1,x_2)\le t\,\},
where ||\cdot|| denotes distance to the nearest integer. Define
\omega_+(\Theta)=\sup\{\gamma>0: \liminf_{t\to\infty} t^\gamma\psi_+(t)<\infty\}.
What is the exact value of
\inf_{\Theta}\omega_+(\Theta),
where the infimum is over all such \Theta? Equivalently, given Schmidt's lower bound \omega_+(\Theta)\ge \varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2 for every \Theta and Moshchevitin's upper bound \inf_{\Theta}\omega_+(\Theta)\le \sigma, where \sigma is the largest real root of x^4-2x^2-4x+1\approx 1.94696, determine the true optimal exponent in this positive-integer two-variable problem.
justification: Your draft is already close to the first problem discussed in Section 1, but the nearest paper-faithful target is not the original Schmidt conjecture by itself. Because your draft explicitly asks whether the optimal exponent is \varphi, \sigma, or something in between, it is best interpreted as the sharpened open problem that remains after Theorem 1.3: determine the exact value of \inf_{\Theta}\omega_+(\Theta).

refined_question: Let p be a prime, let U\subset (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times be a multiplicative subgroup, let v\in (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times, and put R=vU. The paper’s main theorem, Theorem 3.1, concerns the first-order asymptotics of ln f(n). Your draft is not aiming at that theorem itself; rather, it matches the separate open problem stated later in Section 5, where the authors explicitly single out monotonicity of f(n) as a desirable simpler task. So the sharp, paper-faithful refinement is the monotonicity question for the exact sequence f(n)=|T(n)|, with the quantifier stated explicitly as n ≥ 1. ([combinatorics.org](https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/download/v19i2p18/pdf/))

refined_question: For each positive integer n, let T(n) be the set of Wilf partitions of n, written canonically as pairs (m, p) = ((m_1, ..., m_r), (p_1, ..., p_r)) with r >= 1, m_1, ..., m_r distinct positive integers, 1 <= p_1 < ... < p_r distinct part sizes, and sum_{i=1}^r m_i p_i = n. Define the involution σ_n : T(n) -> T(n) by σ_n((m, p)) = (p_π, m_π), where π is the permutation of {1, ..., r} such that m_{π(1)} < ... < m_{π(r)}. The draft is therefore very close in intent, but it needs the paper's canonical pair notation, the exact definition of the permutation π, and the correction that the reordering is to make the part-size list increasing after the swap.

original_question: Consider the one-dimensional recurrence/transience criterion for excited random walks under the assumptions that the family of cookie stacks is i.i.d., that there is a deterministic bound M with M(z) <= M almost surely for every site z (so each site has only boundedly many non-placebo cookies), and that every direction remains possible at every site and visit in the weak-ellipticity sense. Can the i.i.d. assumption on the cookie stacks be weakened to the stationary-and-ergodic assumption while keeping the same recurrence/transience conclusion?

M(z)≤M for every z in Z, where M(z):=inf{j in N_0 : ω(z,e,i)=1/2 for all e in {-1,+1} and all i>j} ((BD)); and that for each z in Z and e in {-1,+1}, P[forall i in N : ω(z,e,i)>0]>0 ((WEL)). original_question: For dimension d >= 2, suppose the family of cookie stacks is i.i.d. and uniformly elliptic, meaning there exists kappa > 0 such that every transition probability ω(z,e,i) is at least kappa almost surely. Must the excited random walk always fall into one of the two global behaviors: recurrence, meaning every site is visited infinitely often almost surely, or transience, meaning no site is visited infinitely often almost surely?

original_question: Fix a possibly infinite collection of affine constraints {(M_1,sigma_1),(M_2,sigma_2),...} over F2. original_question: For each constant delta > 0, do s^{-O(1)}-biased densities delta-fool all size-s DNF formulas; equivalently, if f : {0,1}^n -> {-1,1} is computable by a size-s DNF and phi is an s^{-O(1)}-biased density on {0,1}^n, must |E_{x~{0,1}^n}[f(x)] - E_{y~phi}[f(y)]| <= delta?

refined_question: For every fixed constant δ > 0, does there exist a constant c = c(δ) > 0 such that, for all n and s ≥ 1, every probability distribution φ on {0,1}^n satisfying |E_{y∼φ}[χ_S(y)]| ≤ s^{-c} for every nonempty S ⊆ [n] δ-fools every DNF formula on n variables with at most s terms? Equivalently, if f : {0,1}^n → {-1,1} is computable by a DNF of size at most s and φ is s^{-c}-biased in the above sense, must |E_{x∼U_n}[f(x)] - E_{y∼φ}[f(y)]| ≤ δ?
justification: In arXiv:1204.6447 itself, the exact target is the survey item "ε-biased Sets for DNFs," and your draft is essentially a near-verbatim paraphrase of that item. The survey’s statement is brief, so I made explicit the hidden quantifier inside s^{-O(1)}, the meaning of ε-bias via nontrivial parity characters, the role of the uniform distribution U_n, and the standard term-count meaning of DNF size. I did not broaden the scope to width-w DNFs, read-once DNFs, or AC0. The nearby context in the survey and in DETT10 shows why this exact sharpening is the paper-faithful one: DETT10 proves general-DNF fooling only for much smaller bias, namely roughly exp(-O(log^2(s/δ) log log(s/δ))), proves a stronger polynomial-bias result only for read-once DNFs, and gives lower bounds showing that for general DNFs one needs bias at least m^{-Ω(log(1/δ))} in the low-error regime. So the open problem is specifically whether polynomially small bias in s suffices once δ is fixed as a constant.

refined_question: Open problem. Let X be a Banach space, and let K(X) denote the Banach algebra of compact operators on X, equipped with composition as multiplication and the operator norm topology. The paper first asks in Problem 4.6 whether these same two strong polarized relations are consistent for a strong limit singular λ in general, then immediately sharpens the question by observing that when cf(λ)=ω one may violate the local continuum hypothesis at λ while still keeping 2^θ=θ^+ below λ, leading exactly to Problem 4.7. Definition 1.1 is needed to make the arrow notation self-contained. Section 5 confirms that the two cases λ^+ and 2^λ are the precise special cases the authors regard as most interesting in the later main theorem, although the later positive results are obtained under different hypotheses and so do not replace Problem 4.7.

original_question: Suppose λ is singular and 2^λ > λ^+. Does ZFC prove that for every α < λ^+, every 2-coloring of λ^+ × λ has a monochromatic rectangle A×B with |A| = α and |B| = λ, i.e. \((λ^+ over λ) → (α over λ)^(1,1)_2\) for all α < λ^+?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Problem 4.8: whether, for a singular cardinal λ with 2^λ > λ^+, one has \binom{\lambda^+}{\lambda} \to \binom{\alpha}{\lambda}^{1,1}_2 for every \alpha < \lambda^+.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the paper’s actual target: λ is singular, the hypothesis is 2^λ > λ^+, the question quantifies over every α < λ^+, it is about 2-colorings of λ^+ × λ, and the desired conclusion is the polarized relation \binom{\lambda^+}{\lambda} \to \binom{\alpha}{\lambda}^{1,1}_2.

refined_question: Assume that λ is a singular cardinal with λ > cf(λ) and 2^λ > λ^+. Is it a theorem of ZFC that for every ordinal α < λ^+ and every coloring c: λ^+ × λ → 2, there exist sets A ⊆ λ^+ and B ⊆ λ of order types α and λ, respectively, such that c is constant on A × B; equivalently in the paper’s notation, does \binom{\lambda^+}{\lambda} \to \binom{\alpha}{\lambda}^{1,1}_2 hold for every α < λ^+?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 4, Problem 4.8 almost verbatim. Right before that problem, the paper recalls a weaker theorem from [S3]: if λ is strong limit singular and 2^λ > λ^+, then one already gets \binom{\lambda^+}{\lambda} \to \binom{\lambda+1}{\lambda}^{1,1}_\theta for every \theta < cf(λ). Problem 4.8 then asks for exactly the strengthening your draft is trying to express, namely whether one can replace that weaker conclusion by \binom{\lambda^+}{\lambda} \to \binom{\alpha}{\lambda}^{1,1}_2 for every α < λ^+ under only singularity of λ and 2^λ > λ^+. Theorem 2.7 gives the nearby comparison case where this stronger conclusion is already known in ZFC when λ is a limit of measurable cardinals. Definition 1.1 supplies the paper’s monochromatic-rectangle reading of polarized notation in the strong case, and Corollary 5.3 shows that the paper later proves consistency of an even stronger full relation by forcing, rather than resolving Problem 4.8 in ZFC.

refined_question: Prove or disprove the following 'increasing columns' conjecture for the classical pattern 1324: for every n,k ∈ Z_{≥0}, if S_n^k(1324) denotes the number of permutations π ∈ S_n that avoid 1324 and satisfy inv(π)=k, then S_n^k(1324) ≤ S_{n+1}^k(1324). justification: The draft is aiming at the paper's Section 3 discussion of 1324-avoiders with a fixed number of inversions, not at the paper's broader Introduction-level conjectures about layered patterns. In the cited source that Section 3 is summarizing, the exact open problem is Conjecture 13, which asserts monotonicity in n of the fixed-k counts S_n^k(1324). The numerical bound e^{π√(2/3)} is not itself posed there as the main conjecture; rather, Theorem 17 proves that this bound follows from Conjecture 13. Proposition 15 supplies the combinatorial description of the eventual fixed-k column values that drives the proof. Therefore the paper-faithful refinement should ask for a proof or refutation of the monotonicity conjecture, with the e^{π√(2/3)} bound stated as its conditional consequence.

justification: The arXiv paper 1210.7320 is a survey, not the original source of the conjecture. In Section 3, it explicitly says that [23] conjectures that the number of 1324-avoiders of length n with a fixed number k of inversions is increasing as a function of n. The cited paper [23] gives the formal version as Conjecture 13 ('Increasing columns'), after defining inversions and the notation S_n^k(τ). Its nearby Proposition 15 supplies the important hidden context that for fixed k the column is already constant for n ≥ k+2, and Theorem 17 explains why this monotonicity matters by deriving the improved upper bound for L(1324) from it. So your draft is very close, but it should be sharpened to an explicit weak inequality with full notation and definitions.

refined_question: Prove or refute the following conjecture. For each integer k ≡ 1 (mod 4), let λ_k be the classical layered permutation of length k obtained as the direct sum of decreasing blocks with sizes (1,2,...,2,3,2,...,2,1), so that there are (k-5)/4 blocks of size 2 on each side of the central block of size 3. refined_question: Let M be a real analytic n-dimensional manifold, and let f and g be real analytic vector fields on M, not assumed generic. Consider the fixed-endpoint time-optimal problem for the single-input control-affine system q̇ = f(q) + u g(q), |u| ≤ 1, with measurable controls u and Lipschitz admissible trajectories. Assume that two points q0, q1 ∈ M are connected by at least one time-optimal trajectory. In the nontrivial case n ≥ 3, must there exist a time-optimal trajectory from q0 to q1 whose set of switching points—i.e. points where the trajectory is not smooth—does not have positive measure?
justification: The draft is aimed at Section I.B, not at the generic C∞ problem in Section I.A. In Section I.B the paper first fixes the real-analytic control-affine system and explains that, although arbitrary optimal trajectories may be very irregular, one hopes that among all time-optimal trajectories with the same endpoints there is at least one with better switching behavior. After recalling that finite switching is known in dimension 2 but fails already in dimension 3 via the Fuller phenomenon, the paper states a stronger main open question about countably many switching points and then immediately records the weaker unresolved issue that matches your draft: whether one can avoid a positive-measure set of switching points. The refined question therefore keeps your weaker target, but adds the precise system, admissibility, analyticity, endpoint quantifier, non-generic scope, and the dimension context needed to make it faithful and stand-alone.

original_question: For incompressible fluid dynamics, especially at very large Reynolds number where viscosity is very small, is violent turbulence fundamentally caused by rough dependence on initial data rather than ordinary sensitive dependence on initial data? Does this mechanism, or the very large derivative of the Navier-Stokes solution map in the high-Reynolds-number regime, explain why sufficiently large-Reynolds-number turbulence develops violently in short time?

To make the question fully stand-alone and faithful to that solution, one must state it for each fixed complex dimension, include the preferred complex orientation in the oriented cases, and make explicit that the answer is only well-posed up to the universal Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch relations chi_p = Td_p. The refined version stays close to the original intent of Problem 31 while incorporating exactly the distinctions and exception actually used in the paper, especially the exclusion of complex dimension 2 in the unoriented diffeomorphism case.

original_question: Suppose α is an endomorphism of a group G such that for every group H and every homomorphism f: G → H, there exists an endomorphism βf of H such that βf f = f α. Must α then be either an inner automorphism of G or the trivial endomorphism? This is Question 5 in(G. M. Bergman, Publ. Matem., 56(2012), 91–126).
target_in_paper: Problem 21.14 in arXiv:1401.0300 (The Kourovka Notebook, New Problems, 21st issue), which records Bergman’s group-theoretic open problem in the simplified equivalent form.
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the Kourovka Notebook statement very closely: it quantifies over all groups H and all homomorphisms f: G → H, uses the commuting condition βf ∘ f = f ∘ α, and asks exactly the same dichotomy that appears in Problem 21.14, namely whether α must be an inner automorphism or the trivial endomorphism. It also correctly identifies the underlying source as Bergman’s Question 5.

refined_question: Let G be an arbitrary group and let α ∈ End(G). Assume that for every group H and every homomorphism f: G → H, there exists an endomorphism βf ∈ End(H) such that βf ∘ f = f ∘ α. Must it follow that either α is conjugation by some element s ∈ G (equivalently, α(g) = sgs^{-1} for all g ∈ G), or α is the trivial endomorphism g ↦ 1_G of G?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, in Bergman’s original formulation: if α ∈ End(G) is such that for every object f: G → H of the comma category (G↓Group) there exists βf ∈ End(H) with βf ∘ f = f ∘ α, must α be inner in the sense of Definition 4; that is, can the endomorphisms βf be chosen so that for every commuting triangle G --f--> H1 --h--> H2 one has βh∘f ∘ h = h ∘ βf, i.e. so that the family (βf) defines an endomorphism of the forgetful functor (G↓Group) → Group?
justification: In arXiv:1401.0300 the problem appears as Problem 21.14, already restated in the simplified form used in your draft: the conclusion is phrased directly as 'inner automorphism or trivial endomorphism.' Bergman’s original paper, however, formulates the question as a coherence problem for the family (βf) over the comma category (G↓Group). Theorem 1 identifies coherent systems of automorphisms with conjugation by a unique element of G, Theorem 2 packages this as automorphisms of the forgetful functor, Corollary 3 shows that allowing endomorphisms adds only the trivial case, and Definition 4/Question 5 package the open problem in exactly that language. So the sharp paper-faithful stand-alone question is your draft with the implicit definitions made explicit, while the only alternate formulation worth giving is the paper-explicit functorial one.

Algebra, 319, no. 2(2008), 800–805), as well as for n ⩽ 5 when p ̸= 2(M. Konvisser, D. Jonah, J. Algebra, 34(1975), 309–330). The answer to both questions is “no” for n ⩾ (p+9)/2 when p ⩾ 5(for p ⩾ 7 due to G. Glauberman, Contemp. Math., 524(2010), 61–65; for p = 3, 5 due to Ya. G. Berkovich, J. Algebra, 248, no. 2(2002), 472–553). Thus, the only open cases for p ⩾ 5 are n = 6 for p = 5, and n = (p + 3)/2, (p + 5)/2, (p + 7)/2 for p > 5.

original_question: We say that a product XY = {xy | x ∈ X, y ∈ Y } of two subsets X, Y of a group G is direct if for every z ∈ XY there are unique x ∈ X, y ∈ Y such that z = xy. Is there an infinite group G such that every subset A ⊆ G satisfies the following property: all the maximal subsets B for which the product AB is direct have the same cardinality? Note that for checking the property for a given infinite group G, it suffices to consider only those subsets A ⊆ G for which |A| = |G \ A|. Indeed, the property is equivalent to A−1 A ∩ BB −1 = {1} and A−1 AB = G, and these imply |G| = |A||B|, since G is infinite. Now, if |A| < |G \ A|, then |A| < |G|, and so |B| = |G|; and if |A| > |G \ A|, then A−1 A = G, and so |B| = 1, for all B satisfying the property.

original_question: Let p be a prime number. original_question: The paper rigorously derives several NLS-type asymptotic models from Maxwell's equations and justifies them on times of order T/epsilon only while the approximating NLS-type solution stays bounded, which in the standard focusing case means times strictly before the focusing time T_foc. target_in_paper: Section 4.5, Open Problem 10: the problem of extending the rigorous Maxwell-to-NLS-type approximation beyond the pre-focusing regime, specifically to a diffractive time scale [0, T/epsilon] with T >= T_foc.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's actual long-time approximation issue: Section 3 proves O(epsilon)-type justifications of several NLS-type models derived from Maxwell's equations on intervals [0, T/epsilon], and Section 4.5 explains that for the standard focusing cubic NLS this argument only gives T < T_foc because the justification requires boundedness of the approximating envelope and the error constant blows up as T approaches the focusing time. Your draft also correctly captures the paper's motivation that the various models only begin to differ in a relevant way near focusing, so pre-focusing justifications are not sharp enough.

refined_question: Under the same wave-packet and polarization assumptions as in Section 3—namely, for Maxwell initial data U|_{t=0} = u_0(x)e^{ik·x/epsilon} + c.c. with u_0 in B = H^{t_0}(R^d)^n (t_0 > d/2) or in the Wiener algebra W(R^d)^n, satisfying u_0 = pi_1(k)u_0 + epsilon r and the standing hypotheses of the corresponding derivation—can one rigorously justify at least one of the NLS-type approximations derived from Maxwell's equations in Section 3, in the same sense as the paper's O(epsilon) error estimates for U_app(t,x) = u_app(t,x)e^{i(k·x-omega t)/epsilon} + c.c., on a diffractive time interval [0, T/epsilon] with T >= T_foc, where T_foc is the focusing time of the standard cubic focusing NLS (1)?
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of Section 4.5, Open Problem 10. The paper first sets up the exact Maxwell Cauchy problems (20)-(23) and then proves in Section 3 that several derived NLS-type envelope models approximate the exact Maxwell evolution with O(epsilon) error on [0, T/epsilon]. Section 4.5 then explains why this is not sharp in the focusing regime: for the standard cubic focusing NLS, the justification requires boundedness of the approximate envelope, so the constant in the estimate blows up as T approaches the focusing time T_foc; moreover, the paper notes that the various models only meaningfully separate near focusing. The official question is therefore precisely whether one can justify one such model on [0, T/epsilon] with T >= T_foc. Your draft is already close, but to be fully stand-alone and paper-faithful it should explicitly mention the Maxwell/NLS approximation framework, the O(epsilon) notion of justification from Section 3, and the exact meaning of T_foc.

original_question: In bootstrap algebraic multigrid, how should one define a form of compatible relaxation together with a convergence-rate estimate derived from the compatible-relaxation factor rho_cr so that, for a chosen interpolation strategy, the estimate accurately predicts the performance of the resulting two-grid method?
target_in_paper: Section 2, first of the two explicit open compatible-relaxation questions: "How to define an appropriate form of CR and related convergence rate estimate from ρcr that accurately predicts the performance of the resulting two-grid method for a given interpolation strategy?"
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s actual formulation. It correctly identifies the BAMG/compatible-relaxation setting, the need to define a suitable form of CR, the role of the CR factor ρcr, and the goal of predicting the quality of the resulting two-grid method for a specified interpolation strategy. In substance, it is almost a paraphrase of the paper’s first explicit open CR question.
missing_details: ["The paper presents this as an open research question in Section 2, not as an established result or design rule.", "The ambient setting is a linear system Ax = b with A ∈ ℂ^{n×n}; the associated two-grid method uses a fine-grid relaxation M and transfer operators R : ℂ^n → ℂ^{n_c} and P : ℂ^{n_c} → ℂ^n.", "In the paper, compatible relaxation means a relaxation scheme that keeps the coarse-grid variables invariant; in the more general HCR setting, the coarse variables can also be averages defined by a matrix X rather than a literal subset of fine variables.", "ρcr is defined in nearby context as an approximation to the asymptotic convergence rate of CR after ν CR iterations in Algorithm 2.1.", "The target of the prediction should be stated quantitatively as the convergence rate/factor of the resulting two-grid method, rather than the broader word performance.", "The paper stresses that no precise general relation between a CR iteration’s convergence rate and the resulting two-grid convergence is known in general; special predictive variants already exist only in specific cases such as F-relaxation and HCR.", "If one uses the nearby HCR reformulation, the prediction quality depends on the averaging matrix X; the paper notes that a suitable choice is X = P^H for a sufficiently accurate and stable interpolation operator P, and this P need not coincide with the interpolation actually used in the AMG solver."]
refined_question: For a linear system Ax = b with A ∈ ℂ^{n×n}, a fixed fine-grid relaxation scheme M, a coarse-variable choice C ⊂ Ω (or, more generally, coarse averages defined by an averaging matrix X in the HCR setting), and a specified interpolation strategy P for the associated AMG two-grid solver, how should one define a compatible-relaxation process and an associated estimate based on its asymptotic convergence factor ρcr so that this estimate accurately predicts the convergence factor of the resulting two-grid method?
justification: The draft matches the first explicit open problem stated at the end of the compatible-relaxation discussion in Section 2 (p. 120). The nearby context defines CR as relaxation that keeps coarse variables invariant and introduces HCR as a general variant whose rate can, with suitable coarse-variable averages, accurately predict achievable two-grid convergence (Section 1, p. 115). Section 2 then defines ρcr through Algorithm 2.1 as an approximation to the asymptotic CR rate (p. 118), and immediately after the open question explains that the precise general relation between CR convergence and two-grid convergence is not known, though F-relaxation and HCR give special predictive cases; it also records the HCR operator and the role of X = P^H in prediction sharpness (p. 121). Those are the paper-faithful details needed to make the question stand alone without broadening it beyond the authors’ stated intent.

Define subset(L_d) to be the maximum cardinality of a subset S ⊂ L_d such that no two distinct unordered pairs of points of S determine the same positive Euclidean distance; equivalently, every nonzero distance spanned by S occurs at most once. Find the asymptotic value of subset(L_d) as n -> infinity.
justification: The draft is clearly targeting the lattice-specialized open problem from the section on subsets with no repeated distances, not the general function subset_d(n). The paper first defines subset(P) as the largest subset of a point set P in which no positive distance is repeated, then asks for the asymptotic value of subset(L_d) when L_d is a d-dimensional integer lattice of side length n^(1/d). The immediately surrounding context records the known bounds subset(L_d) = Ω(n^(2/(3d))) and subset(L_d) = O(n^(1/d)); the upper bound comes from the earlier higher-dimensional observation that such a lattice determines only O(n^(2/d)) distinct distances. To make the question stand alone while staying faithful to the paper, one must specify the Euclidean ambient space, the exact pairwise nonrepetition condition, the lattice as a section of Z^d, and the asymptotic regime n -> infinity for fixed d. The planar case d = 2 is treated separately just before this higher-dimensional lattice problem.

refined_question: Let X be a complex separable Banach space. Assume that X has the maximal regularity property (MRP), i.e. every negative generator of an analytic C0-semigroup on X has maximal regularity. Must X be isomorphic to a Hilbert space?

Later, in the notes/open-problems discussion, the paper asks whether this Hilbert-space characterization remains true for separable Banach spaces, and if not, whether it at least remains true for (separable) UMD-spaces. Your draft is therefore aimed at that separable-space open problem, but it is not yet paper-faithful because it replaces the official MRP formulation by an R-sectorial one without imposing the UMD hypothesis, and it adds the Schauder-basis class, which the paper does not isolate as the formal open problem. The closest sharp stand-alone question is thus the separable-Banach-space MRP problem, with the UMD/R-sectorial version as the justified alternate formulation.

refined_question: Let m and n be integers with m≥3 and n≥2. For a nonnegative order-m, dimension-n tensor A, let γ(A) denote its primitive degree, i.e. the least positive integer r such that T_A^r(x)>0 for every nonzero x∈R_+^n. Define E(m,n):={k∈N : there exists a nonnegative primitive tensor A of order m and dimension n with γ(A)=k}. Determine E(m,n); in particular, is it true that E(m,n)={1,2,...,(n-1)^2+1}?

justification: The closest paper-faithful target is not a single theorem statement but the final paragraph of Section 1.1, where the author explicitly lists the remaining open problems after proving Theorems 1.3 and 1.6. So the mathematically sharp stand-alone reformulation of the draft is a single question about the necessity of exactly those extra assumptions, stated in the paper’s original notation and scope.

refined_question: Let (X, ω) be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension n, and let PSH(X, ω) denote the set of ω-plurisubharmonic functions. For φ ∈ PSH(X, ω), say that φ belongs to DMA(X, ω) if there exists a Radon measure μ on X such that, for every sequence φ_j ∈ PSH(X, ω) ∩ C∞(X) decreasing to φ on X, the measures (ω + dd^cφ_j)^n converge weakly to μ; in that case one writes (ω + dd^cφ)^n := μ. Characterize the class DMA(X, ω), i.e. give necessary and sufficient conditions for an ω-psh function on a compact Kähler manifold to belong to the global domain of definition of the complex Monge-Ampère operator.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, characterize those φ ∈ PSH(X, ω) for which the same weak-limit property holds when one replaces smooth ω-psh approximants by arbitrary bounded ω-psh approximants decreasing to φ; in particular, one may test this using the canonical truncations φ_j = max(φ, -j).
justification: The draft is aiming directly at Question 5 in §1.1.3. The paper first defines DMA(X, ω) in Definition 1.3 via weak convergence of (ω + dd^cφ_j)^n along every decreasing smooth ω-psh approximation, then immediately defines the local counterpart DMAloc(X, ω) in Definition 1.4 and stresses that the global and local domains are different. The official open problem is then stated exactly as 'Characterize DMA(X, ω).' The nearby discussion supplies the intended scope: DMA(X, ω) is a strict subclass of PSH(X, ω); Lelong numbers give an obstruction to membership; and the known subclasses E(X, ω) and DMAloc(X, ω) are both contained in DMA(X, ω). So your draft has the right target, but it needs the paper’s own definition of DMA(X, ω), the universal approximation quantifier, and the explicit global-vs-local distinction to be fully stand-alone and faithful.

refined_question: Let G be a finite abelian group of order n, written additively, let p be the smallest prime divisor of n, and let h,m be positive integers such that m <= p < hm-h+1. Since Proposition 1.2 gives rho(G,m,h) = min{p, hm-h+1} = p in this range, is it true that an m-subset A satisfies |hA| = p if and only if A is contained in a coset a+H of some subgroup H <= G with |H| = p?

justification: The draft is targeting the signed-sumset open problem stated at the end of Section 0.4. The exact official formulation in the paper is Conjecture 0.4.5. refined_question: Let H be an n x n real symmetric or complex Hermitian random matrix drawn from an ensemble E, and let A be an isospectral eigenvalue algorithm, discrete or continuous, whose evolution X starts at H and converges to diagonal form. refined_question: Let Σ and Δ be finite alphabets, and let h, g: Σ* -> Δ* be morphisms. original_question: Given a Post Correspondence Problem instance (h, g), can one decide whether it satisfies the unique equality continuation property, namely that for every word u and every pair of distinct letters a and b, the comparabilities h(ua) ⊲⊳ g(ua) and h(ub) ⊲⊳ g(ub) imply h(u) = g(u)?
target_in_paper: Section 3.5, Question 3.5.05.2: the decidability of whether a given PCP instance is a unique equality continuation instance.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly targets the second open problem in the paper, not the neighboring question about deciding PCP itself on that class. It also states the right property: for a fixed prefix u and two distinct next letters a,b, if both extensions ua and ub make h and g comparable, then one must already have h(u)=g(u). This is exactly the paper’s unique equality continuation condition (UC3), just written in stand-alone form.

refined_question: Let A and B be finite alphabets, and let h,g:A*→B* be morphisms, viewed as an instance I=(h,g) of the Post Correspondence Problem. Call two words x,y∈B* comparable if one is a prefix of the other. Is there an algorithm that, given I, decides whether I is a unique equality continuation instance, meaning that for every u∈A* and every pair of distinct letters a,b∈A, the comparabilities h(ua) and g(ua), and h(ub) and g(ub), force h(u)=g(u)?
equivalent_formulation: Is it decidable whether or not an instance of the PCP satisfies the property (UC3)?
justification: The draft matches the survey’s Question 3.5.05.2 almost verbatim: it asks for recognition of the unique equality continuation property, not for decidability of PCP restricted to that class. The survey gives exactly this formulation in Section 3.5, and the original Halava–Harju–Karhumäki–Latteux paper defines the same property as UC3 and immediately leaves as open the question whether one can decide if a PCP instance satisfies UC3. The only substantive omissions in the draft are the finite alphabets, the morphism typing h,g:A*→B*, the quantifier domains u∈A* and a,b∈A, and the explicit definition of comparability as the prefix relation in either direction. equivalent_formulation: Paper-proved alternate formulation: characterize simple nonplanar \overline{C_6}-free bricks, where \overline{C_6} is the triangular prism and '\overline{C_6}-free' means having no conformal minor isomorphic to \overline{C_6}; by Section 3.2, any simple nonplanar brick distinct from the Petersen graph is solid if and only if it is \overline{C_6}-free, and together with Theorem 1.33 this yields that, apart from the staircases of order 0 mod 4, the tricorn, and the Petersen graph, a simple brick is solid if and only if it is \overline{C_6}-free.

correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the binary setting, the extremal function XNL(n), the fact that one is counting nonequivalent abelian-square factors rather than occurrences, the use of Parikh vectors to define equivalence, and the intended asymptotic upper bound O(n^(3/2)).

original_question: For a binary linear word of length n, let MDL(n) be the minimum possible number of distinct abelian square factors. Is MDL(n) always equal to floor(n/4)? correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact problem family: binary linear words, distinct abelian-square factors (not occurrences, and not merely inequivalent ones), the conjectured value floor(n/4), and the special extremal-family statement for lengths n = 4k + 3. Moreover, for every integer k >= 0, are the only binary words of length 4k + 3 having exactly k distinct abelian-square factors the words a^(2k+1)ba^(2k+1) and b^(2k+1)ab^(2k+1) (equivalently, a^(2k+1)ba^(2k+1) and its complement)?
justification: This is the nearest official formulation to your draft in arXiv:1802.04481: the survey first separates the linear/circular and distinct/inequivalent counting problems, then states Conjecture 0.5 for the minimum number of distinct abelian squares in binary linear words. Your draft matches that conjecture essentially verbatim. The only stand-alone pieces missing are the formal definition of abelian square, the meaning of 'distinct factor', the binary alphabet/complement convention, and explicit quantifiers. The nearby Dagstuhl abstract cited by Simpson gives the hidden context behind this conjecture: it defines Abelian Square Minimal words and trivial abelian squares, proves the lower bound for words having only trivial abelian squares, and explains why the centered single-b construction yields floor(n/4). However, that source gives only a sufficient reduction to a different conjecture about ASM words; it does not prove an equivalent reformulation of Conjecture 0.5, so no alternate equivalent formulation should be supplied.

refined_question: Let Q_n^d be the space of homogeneous degree-d forms on C^n, with n >= 2 and d >= 3, let X_n^d = {f in Q_n^d : Δ(f) != 0} be the locus of nondegenerate forms, and let Φ : X_n^d -> Q_n^{n(d-2)*} be the associated-form morphism attached to the Milnor algebra M(f) = C[z_1,...,z_n]/(f_{z_1},...,f_{z_n}). justification: The abstract of arXiv:1803.04005 says the paper studies the associated-form morphism for homogeneous degree-d forms with nonvanishing discriminant and connects it to explicit reconstruction from the Tjurina algebra. The introduction of the closely related associated-form papers spells out the exact conjectural formulation: all GL_n-invariant regular functions on X_n^d should be obtainable by pullback along Φ from rational invariants on the space of associated forms. Those same introductions also explain why this gives the homogeneous version of the reconstruction problem: for homogeneous/quasi-homogeneous singularities, Milnor and Tjurina algebras coincide, so recovering a complete invariant system from the associated form is the paper-faithful reformulation of 'explicit reconstruction' here. Hence your draft is directionally right on motivation but substantially broader than the actual scope and wording of the paper. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.04005?utm_source=openai))

original_question: Let Omega be a finite family of convex polytopes in R^n. For each unit vector g in S^{n-1}, define C(g) to be the convex hull of all support faces Arg max_{x in P} <x,g> taken over P in Omega, and define F(Omega) = {C(g) : g in S^{n-1}}. Starting from Omega_0, iterate Omega_i = F(Omega_{i-1}). Which initial finite families Omega_0 have the property that this sequence eventually enters a 2-cycle, meaning that there exists N with Omega_{N+2} = Omega_N?

refined_question: Let Ω_0 be a finite family of convex polytopes in ℝ^n. For each direction g∈S^{n-1} and each P∈Ω, let P_g:=Arg max_{x∈P}⟨x,g⟩ be the support (exposed) face of P in direction g, and define C_Ω(g):=conv(⋃_{P∈Ω}P_g). Characterize those initial finite families Ω_0 for which there exists N∈ℕ such that Ω_{N+2}=Ω_N; that is, characterize exactly which collections eventually fall into a cycle of period dividing 2 under this Demyanov-Ryabova conversion, in a way that extends/generalizes the special cases already known. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))
justification: This rewrite follows the closest official formulation in the paper itself. The introduction says that Section 8 recalls the Demyanov-Ryabova conjecture, notes that it has been answered negatively, and presents a new revised question. Section 8 then gives the exact notation C(g), F(Ω), and Ω_i, restates the original eventual-two-cycle claim as “for a sufficiently large N we have Ω_{N+2}=Ω_N,” and finally asks for a characterization of the collections of polytopes that do yield two-cycles. The references identify [23] as the original source of the conjecture, [24] and [25] as the previously proved special cases to be extended/generalized, and [26] as the counterexample. The paper does not provide an explicit equivalent reformulation of this revised open question, so no alternate formulation should be added. ([espace.curtin.edu.au](https://espace.curtin.edu.au/bitstream/handle/20.500.11937/81338/81402.pdf))

justification: In this paper, the relevant target is the unlabeled open problem in Section 9 rather than any numbered conjecture from another article. Section 9 first defines a net (or unfolding) of a 3-polytope as what results from cutting along edges so that the connected shape can be flattened into the plane, and then states Dürer’s conjecture as the claim that any polytope has a nonoverlapping net. See [35, 34] for numerical evidence supporting Conjecture 16.3 in the case N = D = 1 and d ∈ {2, 3}, including conjectural values for the constants. We also note that the Zariski density assumption in Conjecture 16.3 is necessary. For ex- ample, the map f = [X 2 , Y 2 , γZ 2 ] has height roughly h(γ), while the f -orbit of the point P = [α, 1, 0] has canonical height ĥf (P ) = h(α), so we can make hM (f ) arbitrarily large while ĥf (P ) remains bounded. Ingram [116] and Looper [155] have proven weak versions of Conjecture 16.3 for polynomial maps f of P1 , where the constants depend also on the number of primes of bad reduction of f.

original_question: Consider the exterior Robin boundary value problem for the unit sphere in R^3: find a harmonic function w(φ, θ, r), defined for r > 1, 2π-periodic in θ, twice continuously differentiable, satisfying Laplace’s equation together with the boundary conditions lim_{r→1+} ||α w(φ, θ, r) + β ∂w/∂r(φ, θ, r) − h(φ, θ)||_{L^2(S)} = 0 and lim_{r→∞} w(φ, θ, r) = 0, where h ∈ L^2(S), S is the unit sphere, and α, β are chosen so that α − β(k + 1) ≠ 0 for every nonnegative integer k. For this problem, the boundary operator obtained from the solution formula is not a semigroup unless β = 0 (the Dirichlet case) or α = 0 (the Neumann case). In the semigroup setting for the Dirichlet and Neumann problems, the key tool relating approximation behavior and ergodic behavior is the interconnection theorem λR(λ; A^{-1})f = f − λ^{-1}R(λ^{-1}; A)f, where A is the infinitesimal generator of a semigroup. Does there exist an analogous interconnection relation for the Robin problem, or more generally when the relevant operator A is not the generator of a semigroup of operators, that could play the same role in establishing counterparts of the equivalences involving the resolvents and inverse/ergodic assertions from Theorems 1.1 and 2.1?
target_in_paper: The draft is aiming at the paper's stated novel open problem: to find a Robin-case substitute for the semigroup-based interconnection machinery that works for the exterior Dirichlet and Neumann problems, even though the exterior Robin solution operators for the unit sphere in R^3 do not form a semigroup.

refined_question: Let S be the unit sphere in R^3, let h in L^2(S), and let alpha, beta be fixed real constants such that alpha - beta(k+1) != 0 for every k in N_0. original_question: When the modified Macdonald superpolynomial H_Lambda(q, t) is expanded in the Schur superpolynomial basis as H_Lambda(q, t) = sum_Omega K_{Omega,Lambda}(q, t) s_Omega, are all coefficients K_{Omega,Lambda}(q, t) polynomials in q and t with nonnegative integer coefficients?

original_question: Can the number of balanced vertices of a geodesic net in the Euclidean plane be bounded above by a function of only two quantities: the number of unbalanced vertices and the total imbalance? Here the total imbalance is the sum, over all unbalanced vertices, of the norms of their imbalance vectors.
target_in_paper: Section 3.4, Conjecture 3.4.1 (M. Gromov) in the arXiv version of the paper.
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper’s official formulation. It correctly identifies the ambient space (the Euclidean plane), the object of study (a geodesic net, not an arbitrary graph), the quantity to be bounded (the number of balanced vertices), and the two controlling parameters (the number of unbalanced vertices and the total imbalance). It also gives the paper’s notion of total imbalance in substance: the sum over unbalanced vertices of the norms of their imbalance vectors.
missing_details: ["The paper’s standing conventions matter: all considered geodesic nets are connected.", "Balanced vertices of degree 2 are excluded; this is essential, since the paper notes that one can insert arbitrarily many degree-2 balanced vertices along an edge.", "The paper also imposes the convention that there are no edges between unbalanced vertices.", "To be fully stand-alone, the imbalance vector Imb(v) should be defined explicitly as the sum of the outgoing unit tangent vectors to all edges incident to an unbalanced vertex v.", "The Euclidean-plane specialization should be made explicit: a geodesic net in R^2 is a finite embedded straight-edge graph (distinct edges do not intersect or self-intersect).", "The quantifier should be stated explicitly as the existence of a function F such that for every such geodesic net N, the number of balanced vertices is bounded by F applied to the number of unbalanced vertices and the total imbalance.", "The paper’s conjecture is stated for geodesic nets, not geodesic multinets; the text says an extension to multinets might be plausible, but it is not the official conjecture."]
refined_question: Does there exist a function F : N x [0, infinity) -> N such that every connected geodesic net N in R^2, in the sense and standing conventions of the paper (finite embedded straight-edge graph, no edges between unbalanced vertices, and every balanced vertex of degree at least 3), satisfies #B(N) <= F(|S|, sum_{v in S} ||Imb(v)||), where S is the set of unbalanced vertices, B(N) is the set of balanced vertices, and Imb(v) is the sum of the unit tangent vectors to the edges incident to v, directed away from v?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent special case stated in the discussion immediately after Conjecture 3.4.1: does there exist a function G : N -> N such that any connected geodesic net in R^2, under the same conventions, with n unbalanced vertices and with imbalance exactly 1 at every unbalanced vertex, has at most G(n) balanced vertices?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s official open problem in Section 3.4: Conjecture 3.4.1 (M. Gromov), which states that the number of balanced vertices of a geodesic net in the Euclidean plane is bounded above in terms of the number of unbalanced vertices and the total imbalance (§3.4, p. 13). To make this fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the definitions of imbalance vector and total imbalance from Definition 1.1.1 (§1.1, p. 2), as well as the standing conventions immediately after that definition that all nets under discussion are connected, have no edges between unbalanced vertices, and have no balanced vertices of degree 2 (§1.1, p. 2). That degree restriction is crucial because the paper explicitly says degree-2 balanced vertices can be inserted arbitrarily along an edge. Section 1.2 then specializes the notion to the Euclidean setting, where edges are straight segments in R^2, and records formula (1.2.2), which is later used to derive the one-way auxiliary reformulation Conjecture 3.4.2 (§1.2, pp. 3-4; §3.4, p. 15). I did not use Conjecture 3.4.2 as the alternate formulation because the paper says only that Conjecture 3.4.1 would follow from it, not that the two are equivalent. By contrast, the paper explicitly says that the special case in which every unbalanced vertex has imbalance 1 is equivalent to the full conjecture (discussion immediately after Conjecture 3.4.1, p. 14).

target_in_paper: Conjecture 3.4.2 in §3.4, introduced immediately after Conjecture 3.4.1 as a stronger length/diameter formulation that would imply Gromov's conjectural bound in terms of number of unbalanced vertices and total imbalance.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's exact target. justification: The draft is aiming at Conjecture 3.4.2, not Conjecture 3.4.1, because it asks for a bound in terms of L/D and n rather than in terms of total imbalance and n. original_question: Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold. Does there exist a function f_M, invariant under rescaling of M, with the following property: whenever a geodesic net G on M has total length L, adjusted length L_tilde, diameter D, and n unbalanced vertices, the number of balanced vertices is at most f_M(L_tilde, L/D, n)? Here the adjusted length L_tilde is obtained by summing over all edges e_i the arclength integral of 1 / inj(e_i(s)), where inj(e_i(s)) is the injectivity radius of M at the point e_i(s). In particular, if M has injectivity radius inj > 0, must the number of balanced vertices be at most f_M(L / inj, L / D, n)?

refined_question: Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold. Is the following boundedness conjecture true? There exists a function f_M, depending on M but invariant under rescaling of the metric on M, such that for every finite connected geodesic net G on M, with no edges joining two unbalanced vertices and with every balanced vertex of degree at least 3, if G has n unbalanced vertices, total length L, diameter D, and adjusted total length L_tilde defined by L_tilde := sum over all edges e of the arclength integral integral_e (1/inj_M(x)) ds (equivalently, sum over arc-length parametrized edges e(s) of integral 1/inj_M(e(s)) ds), then the number of balanced vertices of G is at most f_M(L_tilde, L/D, n)? In particular, if M has positive injectivity radius inj(M) > 0, must every such G satisfy that its number of balanced vertices is at most f_M(L/inj(M), L/D, n)?
justification: The draft is targeting the paper's most general boundedness statement, not the earlier Euclidean-plane versions. All of these appear together only in Conjecture 3.4.3. To make the question fully paper-faithful and stand-alone, one must also import the paper's global conventions on geodesic nets from Definition 1.1.1 and the opening of Section 3, especially finiteness, connectedness, the balancing condition, and the exclusion of degree-2 balanced vertices, since otherwise the boundedness question becomes trivialized by edge subdivision.

original_question: Consider the layered geodesic-net construction G_n(phi) built from seven equally spaced outer vertices, an inner seven-vertex layer determined by a deviation parameter phi, and subsequent layers V_i produced by the paper's suspension-and-winging rules. For odd i, define the suspension angle phi_i(phi) as the angle OPv between the ray from the center O of the outer circle to the relevant hook P and the segment Pv for a vertex v in V_i. For even i, define phi_i(phi) as the angle OXv, where X is the third vertex of the equilateral triangle on the relevant outer pair P,Q and v lies in V_i. Does the derivative sequence phi_i'(0) ever repeat, or is it nonrepeating for all i?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 4.5.7 in Section 4.5.1 ("The sequence of suspension angles"), which is the paper's technical conjecture about the derivatives of the suspension-angle sequence in the seven-point star construction; it is used to support Conjecture 4.5.8, not the broader Conjecture 3.3.1.
correct_elements: The draft is already very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies the Section 4 star construction with seven equally spaced outer vertices, the deviation-controlled inner seven-vertex layer, the inductively produced layers V_i, the odd/even split between one-hook and two-hook suspensions, and the fact that the question is about the derivative of the suspension-angle sequence at the symmetric configuration varphi = 0. It also correctly focuses on the exact technical obstruction the paper isolates: whether the derivative sequence repeats.

refined_question: In the seven-point star construction of Section 4 of arXiv:1904.00483, with the paper's fixed algebraic angle alpha in the inner-circle setup and deviation parameter varphi, let varphi_i(varphi) be the suspension angle attached to the i-th layer V_i as defined in Definitions 4.5.1 and 4.5.2 (one-hook suspension for odd i, two-hook suspension for even i, including V_0, the inner circle). Since these angles depend smoothly on varphi by Lemma 4.3.1 and satisfy varphi_i(0) = 0 for all i by Fact 4.5.6, is the derivative sequence (varphi_i'(0))_{i >= 0} pairwise distinct; equivalently, does varphi_i'(0) != varphi_j'(0) hold for every i != j?
justification: The nearest official formulation is Conjecture 4.5.7, not a broader open problem. Section 4.5.1 introduces the suspension-angle sequence precisely to control whether suspension edges overlap under deviation. Lemma 4.5.5 states that if, for fixed varphi, the suspension-angle sequence never repeats, then all edges intersect transversally and hence all weights are 1. Fact 4.5.6 shows that every suspension angle equals 0 at varphi = 0, so the paper isolates the derivative sequence at 0 as the key next object and states Conjecture 4.5.7: that varphi_i'(0) never repeats. The surrounding text then explains that this would imply Conjecture 4.5.8, namely that for small nonzero varphi the actual suspension-angle sequence does not repeat, making the Section 4 star a genuine geodesic net with weight-one edges. The draft captures this target well, but it needs the exact quantifiers, the dependence on the deviation parameter, the smoothness justification, and the explicit pairwise-distinct interpretation of "never repeats" to be fully stand-alone and paper-faithful.

Let t^+(D, J) be the unreduced Sasaki cone of compatible Reeb vector fields, let R(D, J) be its set of rays under transverse scaling (equivalently, one may work in the reduced cone kappa(D, J) = t^+(D, J)/W), and suppose R(D, J) contains an extremal Sasaki ray r_xi, i.e. a ray represented by a compatible Sasakian structure S = (xi, eta, Phi, g) whose scalar curvature has transversely holomorphic (1,0)-gradient, equivalently whose transverse scalar curvature satisfies s_g^T in H_xi or pi_g(s_g^T) = s_g^T. original_question: What is the minimax memory-bounded first-order oracle complexity T_{L,B}(d,M,epsilon) for minimizing a convex L-Lipschitz function F:R^d->R over the Euclidean ball {x: ||x|| <= B} when there exists an optimizer x* with ||x*|| <= B, and an algorithm is allowed T exact first-order oracle calls that each reveal F(x) and a subgradient at x but only M bits of state may be stored between oracle accesses? Equivalently, which query-memory pairs (T,M) are possible or impossible for this problem, preferably up to constant factors and at worst up to polylogarithmic factors in T and M?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Question 1, read together with Section 2's formal definition of T_{L,B}(d,M,epsilon) in Eq. (4) and the possible/impossible tradeoff language.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures almost all of the paper's actual target: the ambient space is R^d, the feasible region is the Euclidean ball, the objective class is convex and L-Lipschitz, an optimizer exists with norm at most B, the oracle returns an exact function value and a subgradient, only M bits of persistent state may be kept between oracle calls, and the goal is the minimax quantity T_{L,B}(d,M,epsilon) or equivalently the possible/impossible (T,M) tradeoff. It also matches the paper's preference for a complete characterization up to constants or at worst polylogarithmic factors. There are no extra algebraic hypotheses here such as degree, homogeneity, characteristic, or nilpotency; this is an optimization problem over Euclidean space.

refined_question: Let A_{M,T} be the class of deterministic first-order algorithms with an M-bit persistent-memory bottleneck between oracle calls: starting from mu_1=0, each round uses a decoder x_t=phi_t(mu_t), receives an exact oracle reply (F(x_t),g_t) with g_t in partial F(x_t), updates mu_{t+1}=psi_t(mu_t,F(x_t),g_t), and finally outputs A(F)=zeta(mu_T), where phi_t, psi_t, and zeta may otherwise use arbitrary real computation. justification: The draft is essentially a paper-faithful restatement of Problem 3.3. Section 3.1 first introduces sign-symmetric signed graphs by the condition Γ is switching isomorphic to -Γ, then states in Theorem 3.2 that every sign-symmetric signed graph has spectrum symmetric about the origin. original_question: For the mod-2 Steenrod algebra A_2 acting on the polynomial algebra P_d = F_2[x_1,…,x_d], determine a minimal generating set of P_d as a left A_2-module for every number of variables d ≥ 5. Equivalently, determine a basis of the quotient space QP_d = F_2 ⊗_{A_2} P_d, which is isomorphic to P_d / A_2^+ P_d, where A_2^+ is the augmentation ideal. In particular, the paper emphasizes that the five-variable case is not yet completely solved and that the general d ≥ 5 case remains open.
target_in_paper: The draft is trying to capture the paper’s unnumbered introductory open problem, namely Peterson’s hit problem at the prime 2: determine, in each degree n ≥ 1, the quotient QP_d = F_2 ⊗_{A_2} P_d ≅ P_d / A_2^+ P_d (equivalently, a minimal A_2-generating set for P_d); the paper notes that this remains open for d ≥ 5, and explains that one may restrict attention to generic degrees n = r(2^t - 1) + 2^t s.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the mod-2 Steenrod algebra setting, the polynomial algebra P_d over F_2, the equivalence between finding minimal A_2-generators of P_d and determining QP_d = F_2 ⊗_{A_2} P_d ≅ P_d / A_2^+ P_d, and the paper’s statement that the case d = 5 is still not fully solved while the general problem is open.

refined_question: At the prime 2, let A_2 be the mod-2 Steenrod algebra and let P_d = F_2[x_1, ..., x_d] ≅ H^*(B(Z/2)^×d; F_2) be the connected unstable left A_2-module on degree-1 generators x_1, ..., x_d, with Sq^1(x_i) = x_i^2, Sq^k(x_i) = 0 for k > 1, and the action extended by the Cartan formula. For each integer d ≥ 5 and each degree n ≥ 1, determine the homogeneous quotient (QP_d)_n, where QP_d := F_2 ⊗_{A_2} P_d ≅ P_d / A_2^+ P_d. Equivalently, and in the standard reduction used in the paper, determine these spaces in the generic degrees n = r(2^t - 1) + 2^t s with integers r, t, s ≥ 0 satisfying 0 ≤ μ(s) < r ≤ d, where μ(m) = min{u ≥ 0 : α(m + u) ≤ u} and α(k) is the number of 1’s in the binary expansion of k.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, determine a minimal set of A_2-generators for P_d degree by degree.
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s opening formulation of Peterson’s hit problem, not at the paper’s specific new theorem on degree 13·2^t - 5. The abstract and §1 state the problem exactly as finding a basis of QP_d in each degree n ≥ 1, equivalently a minimal A_2-generating set for P_d, and say that it remains open for d ≥ 5. The nearby context supplies the unstable-module structure on P_d and the generic-degree reduction n = r(2^t - 1) + 2^t s. Theorems 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 then show that the paper’s actual contribution is only the special five-variable case n = 13·2^t - 5 and its transfer-theoretic consequences, so your draft needed to be sharpened by adding the degree-wise formulation, the exact module structure, and the generic-degree reduction while avoiding the false impression that the paper solves the full d ≥ 5 problem.

target_in_paper: Singer’s conjecture on the injectivity of the d-th algebraic transfer Tr_d.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the object of interest as Singer’s algebraic transfer, gives the right kind of source and target, and asks the right qualitative question: injectivity. justification: The draft is aiming at the introductory Singer-conjecture statement, not at one of the paper’s proved rank-5 theorems. Working at the prime 2, let A_2 be the mod-2 Steenrod algebra, let GL_5 = GL(5,F_2), let P_5 = F_2[x_1, ..., x_5] with |x_i| = 1 and the usual unstable A_2-action, and let QP_5 = F_2 ⊗_{A_2} P_5 ≅ P_5/A_2^+P_5. For the generic degrees n_t = 13·2^t - 5 = 5(2^t - 1) + 8·2^t with t ≥ 2, determine whether the fifth Singer algebraic transfer
Tr_5 : F_2 ⊗_{GL_5} P_{A_2}H_{n_t}(B((Z/2)^5)) → Ext^{5,5+n_t}_{A_2}(F_2,F_2)
is an isomorphism. In the paper this family is reduced to the single degree n_2 = 47: the iterated Kameko map ((gSq^0_*)(5,13·2^t-5))^{t-2} is a GL_5-isomorphism for t ≥ 2, (gSq^0_*)(5,47) : (QP_5)_{47} → (QP_5)_{21} is GL_5-epimorphic, ((QP_5)_{21})^{GL_5} is one-dimensional, and Ext^{5,5+n_t}_{A_2}(F_2,F_2) = <h_{t+1}f_{t-1}> with h_{t+1}f_{t-1} in Im(Tr_5). Thus the concrete unresolved problem is to determine ((QP_5)_{47})^{GL_5}, especially whether (Ker((gSq^0_*)(5,47)))^{GL_5} = 0; and, if not, whether the paper’s more interesting alternative occurs, namely that (Ker((gSq^0_*)(5,47)))^{GL_5} is nontrivial and dim(((QP_5)_{47})^{GL_5}) ≠ 1.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent reduction used explicitly in the paper: for all t ≥ 2, the family above reduces to the single t = 2 case, namely to computing the GL_5-invariants in degree 47, because ((gSq^0_*)(5,13·2^t-5))^{t-2} : (QP_5)_{13·2^t-5} → (QP_5)_{47} is a GL_5-isomorphism; moreover (QP_5)_{47} ≅ Ker((gSq^0_*)(5,47)) ⊕ (QP_5)_{21} as F_2-vector spaces.
justification: The draft is already aimed at the paper’s actual open problem, which is not one of the proved main theorems but the unnumbered discussion at the end of the introduction after Corollary 1.4. There the author proves the t = 0 and t = 1 cases, then explicitly reduces the unresolved t ≥ 2 family to degree 47 via iterated Kameko isomorphisms, uses Theorem 1.2 to identify the unique GL_5-invariant in degree 21, and observes that the Ext target is one-dimensional and detected by classes h_{t+1}f_{t-1}. The draft is therefore close to paper-faithful, but it is not fully stand-alone because it omits the actual transfer source and target, the prime-2 unstable-module conventions, the duality between the transfer source and GL_5-invariants of QP_5, the exact generic-degree parametrization n_t = 13·2^t - 5 = 5(2^t - 1)+8·2^t, and the fact that vanishing of (Ker((gSq^0_*)(5,47)))^{GL_5} is presented by the paper as a sufficient route rather than the sole formulation of the problem. The refined question keeps the scope exactly at the paper’s intended unresolved case and does not broaden it beyond the degree family and reductions actually discussed there.

original_question: Consider the conductivity inclusion problem in dimension n = 2: Omega is a connected open set in R^2 with smooth boundary, k > 0 with k != 1 is fixed, D is an a priori simply connected open subset compactly contained in Omega with smooth boundary, and for boundary data phi the potential u solves div((1 + (k - 1) chi_D) grad u) = 0 in Omega with u = phi on ∂Omega. refined_question: Let X be a context space, A = {1, ..., K} a finite action set, and T the horizon. Consider a finite nested sequence of finite regression classes F_1 ⊂ F_2 ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ F_M = F, where each F_m is a subset of functions X × A → [0,1], and let Π_m = {π_f : f ∈ F_m} with π_f(x) := argmin_{a∈A} f(x,a). In each round t, the learner observes x_t, chooses an action a_t ∈ A, and observes only ℓ_t(a_t), where (x_t, ℓ_t) are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution D on X × [0,1]^A. Assume realizability: there exist m⋆ ∈ [M] and f⋆ ∈ F_{m⋆} such that E[ℓ(a) | x] = f⋆(x,a) for all x ∈ X and a ∈ A. Does there exist, for some α ∈ [1/2, 1), a contextual-bandit algorithm such that for every such nested sequence and every stochastic realizable D, one has E[∑_{t=1}^T ℓ_t(a_t) - ∑_{t=1}^T ℓ_t(π_{f⋆}(x_t))] ≤ O(poly(K, M, log log |F|) · T^α · log^{1-α}|F_{m⋆}|)? If not, can one prove that no algorithm can achieve this guarantee for any α ∈ [1/2, 1)?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, under the realizability assumption, ask for the same regret bound against the class Π_{m⋆} rather than explicitly against the single policy π_{f⋆}, since the paper states that π_{f⋆} is then the optimal unconstrained policy and hence the relevant benchmark in Π_{m⋆}.

original_question: For a fixed dimension d >= 1, what is the optimal constant K_d in the Lieb-Thirring orthonormal-function inequality sum_{n=1}^N int_{R^d} |grad u_n|^2 dx >= K_d int_{R^d} (sum_{n=1}^N |u_n|^2)^(1+2/d) dx, valid for every N and every L^2-orthonormal family u_1,...,u_N in H^1(R^d)?

correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the orthonormal-family kinetic-energy form of the Lieb-Thirring problem at exponent 1+2/d, with the right ambient domain R^d, the right Sobolev space H^1(R^d), and the right uniform quantification over all N and all L^2-orthonormal families. It also correctly asks for the sharp dimension-dependent constant.

refined_question:
For each integer d>=1, let K_d be the optimal constant such that for every N in N and every L^2(R^d;C)-orthonormal family u_1,...,u_N in H^1(R^d), with density rho(x):=sum_{n=1}^N |u_n(x)|^2, one has
sum_{n=1}^N int_{R^d} |grad u_n(x)|^2 dx >= K_d int_{R^d} rho(x)^(1+2/d) dx.
Is the sharp constant K_d equal to the value predicted by the Lieb-Thirring conjecture, namely K_d=K_d^(1) in dimensions d=1,2 and K_d=K_d^cl in dimensions d>=3, where K_d^(1) is the single-function sharp constant (dual to the one-bound-state constant) and K_d^cl is the semiclassical constant?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, if L_{1,d} denotes the sharp constant in the eigenvalue inequality sum_j |lambda_j(-Delta+V)| <= L_{1,d} int_{R^d} V_-(x)^(1+d/2) dx, where V_-:=max{0,-V} and the negative eigenvalues are counted with multiplicity, is it true that L_{1,d}=max{L_{1,d}^{(1)},L_{1,d}^{cl}}?

Thus the paper-faithful stand-alone question must include the density rho, the exact quantifiers, the identification of the sharp constant with the kappa=1 Lieb-Thirring constant, and the dimension-dependent prediction one-function versus semiclassical. Theorem 1.3 is the adjacent opening-section result that helps frame the conjecture and its known evidence/partial results, but the nearest exact target of your draft is Conjecture 1.1 as rewritten by Proposition 1.2.

original_question: Does every homogeneous structure with finite big Ramsey degrees admit a big Ramsey structure, and is there an exact analogue of the Kechris-Pestov-Todorcevic correspondence that links big Ramsey structures with the topological dynamics of automorphism groups?

refined_question: Let K be a countably infinite homogeneous relational structure. Assume that K has finite big Ramsey degrees, meaning that for every finite A in Age(K), the big Ramsey degree T(A) exists. Must K carry a big Ramsey structure, namely a finite expansion K* of K such that every finite substructure of K* has big Ramsey degree 1 and the associated unavoidable colorings (canonical partitions) cohere under embeddings A into B in Age(K)? Moreover, is there an exact correspondence, analogous to the Kechris-Pestov-Todorcevic correspondence, between the existence of such big Ramsey structures for K and the topological dynamics of Aut(K)?
justification: The draft clearly targets Section 6 rather than any earlier theorem: Problem 6.3 asks, almost word for word, whether every homogeneous structure with finite big Ramsey degrees carries a big Ramsey structure and whether there is an exact KPT-type dynamical correspondence. To make that question stand alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the Section 2 conventions and definitions: homogeneous means countably infinite homogeneous relational structure; finite big Ramsey degrees means T(A) exists for every finite A in Age(K); and a big Ramsey structure is described via a finite expansion with degree-1 finite substructures and coherent unavoidable colorings/canonical partitions. The paper also stresses that big Ramsey structures imply canonical partitions, but not conversely in general, so no stronger equivalence should be inserted. Theorems 5.4 and 5.5 provide important positive instances, confirming that the intended target is the global open problem, not a broader neighboring question.

original_question: Consider the single-channel slotted multiple-access problem with n indistinguishable users, where after each slot every user receives perfect feedback giving the exact number of transmitters F[t] on that slot, and the objective is to minimize the expected time until the first successful transmission. The paper develops an efficiently computable policy for arbitrary positive integers n: users randomize on the first slot, use the observed collision size to partition themselves into groups, and then recursively continue with the more favorable subgroup. Is this policy optimal for every positive integer n, or can some other decentralized policy achieve a smaller expected time to first success for some values of n?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1: z_n^* = z_n for all positive integers n.
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right problem class and the right open issue: a single-channel slotted system with n indistinguishable users; exact transmitter-count feedback F[t] after each slot; decentralized/randomized user behavior; the objective of minimizing the expected time to the first success; the paper's first-slot randomization, partition-into-groups, and recursive continuation idea; and the question of whether that policy is globally optimal or can be beaten by some other decentralized policy.
