refined_question: For each positive integer n, consider a single-channel slotted multiple-access system with n indistinguishable users who all know n and who independently implement the same decentralized randomized algorithm, receiving after each slot common perfect feedback F[t] in {0,1,...,n} equal to the exact number of transmitters on that slot; a success occurs iff F[t]=1. Let z_n^* denote the infimum expected time to the first success over all such n-user algorithms. Let z_1=1, z_2=2, and for n>=3 let z_n be the value of the paper's recursively defined divide-and-conquer policy: on slot 1 each user transmits independently with probability p in (0,1); if F[1] is 0 or n, restart; if F[1]=1, stop; and if F[1]=i in {2,...,n-1}, partition the users into the transmitting group of size i and the silent group of size n-i, discard the group with larger continuation value, and recurse on the other group, so that z_n = inf over p in (0,1) of (1 + sum from i=2 to n-1 of min{z_i,z_{n-i}} C(n,i) p^i (1-p)^(n-i)) divided by (1 - p^n - (1-p)^n). Is it true that z_n^* = z_n for every positive integer n?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: is the paper's divide-and-conquer algorithm globally optimal among all decentralized n-user algorithms for every positive integer n, rather than only optimal within its own structured class and rather than only in the proved cases n in {1,2,3,4,6}?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper's main n-user optimality conjecture, not the neighboring open problems about weaker feedback or other model variants. In the introduction, the paper highlights the question 'Is the algorithm of this paper optimal for all values of n?'. Section IV-A defines the recursive divide-and-conquer values z_n and shows they are optimal within that structured class. Section V then defines z_n^* over all decentralized algorithms, states the conjecture z_n=z_n^* for all n, and proves it only for n in {1,2,3,4,6}. So the sharpest stand-alone reformulation is exactly the equality z_n^*=z_n for every positive integer n, with the model and recursion spelled out explicitly.

original_question: Let k be a positive definite kernel on a compact domain X subset R^d, let H_k be the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, and suppose an unknown reward function f belongs to H_k with ||f||_{H_k} <= B. In the online setting, a learner sequentially chooses points x_1, x_2, ... in X, observes noisy rewards y_i = f(x_i) + epsilon_i with i.i.d. sub-Gaussian noise, and may choose each new point using all previous observations. If mu_n(x) and sigma_n(x) are the surrogate Gaussian-process posterior mean and standard deviation after n observations, what is the smallest possible growth rate in n of a confidence-width factor rho_n(delta) for which, with probability at least 1 - delta, the uniform bound |f(x) - mu_n(x)| <= rho_n(delta) sigma_n(x) holds for all x in X? In particular, can the existing online RKHS confidence interval be improved by an O~(sqrt(gamma_n)) factor, where gamma_n is the maximal information gain?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Open Problem (immediately following Theorem 2 on online RKHS confidence intervals).
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's exact target. It also correctly singles out the paper's specific sharpening goal, namely whether the known online confidence width can be improved by an O~(sqrt(gamma_n)) factor.

refined_question: Let X be a compact subset of R^d, let k : X x X -> R be a positive-definite kernel with respect to a finite Borel measure, let H_k be the associated RKHS, and fix lambda > 0. Suppose f in H_k satisfies ||f||_{H_k} <= B, and an online algorithm chooses x_1, x_2, ... adaptively in the sense that x_i is measurable with respect to the past, then observes y_i = f(x_i) + epsilon_i, where the noise variables are i.i.d. and R-sub-Gaussian: E[exp(eta epsilon_i)] <= exp(eta^2 R^2/2) for all eta in R. For the zero-mean GP surrogate with kernel k and regularization lambda, define y_n = (y_1, ..., y_n)^T, k_n(x) = (k(x,x_1), ..., k(x,x_n))^T, K_n = [k(x_i,x_j)]_{i,j=1}^n, mu_n(x) = k_n(x)^T (lambda^2 I_n + K_n)^(-1) y_n, and sigma_n^2(x) = k(x,x) - k_n(x)^T (lambda^2 I_n + K_n)^(-1) k_n(x). What is the smallest asymptotic growth rate, as n increases, of a factor rho_n(delta) such that for every adaptive online design and every delta in (0,1), one has P(for all x in X, |f(x) - mu_n(x)| <= rho_n(delta) sigma_n(x)) >= 1 - delta? In particular, can one improve the current online bound from Theorem 2, rho_n(delta) = B + (R/lambda) sqrt(2(gamma_{n-1} + 1 + log(1/delta))), by removing an O~(sqrt(gamma_n)) factor, where gamma_n := sup_{x_1,...,x_n in X} log det(lambda^2 I_n + K_n), and perhaps reduce the width to O~(d log n)?
justification: The draft is targeting the paper's Section 3 Open Problem almost exactly, rather than a broader regret question. Section 2 supplies the formal assumptions and notation: Assumption 1 gives the RKHS norm bound and sub-Gaussian noise model, Definition 1 gives the online/adaptive measurability condition, and the Surrogate GP Model paragraph defines mu_n and sigma_n. Section 3 then states Theorem 2, the currently known online confidence interval with width B + (R/lambda) sqrt(2(gamma_{n-1} + 1 + log(1/delta))), and immediately after that asks: what is the lowest growth rate of rho_n(delta) with n, and can the width be reduced by an O~(sqrt(gamma_n)) factor? Section 4 further explains the intended sharpening by saying the authors expect the extra sqrt(gamma_n) term in the online width could be replaced by O~(d log n), but this is presented as motivation/discussion rather than as an equivalent reformulation.

original_question: Let (X, H) be a smooth complex projective polarized variety. Does there always exist a class gamma in the numerical Chow ring of the form gamma = e^{-B} * (1, 0, Gamma, gamma_3, ..., gamma_n) together with an upper semicontinuous function f^gamma: R -> R such that every gamma-tilt-semistable object E satisfies the quadratic inequality Q_{s,q}(E) >= 0 for all (s, q) in Delta with q > f^gamma(s)?
target_in_paper: Section 5.3, Conjecture 5.13 (Bayer–Macrì), which the survey explicitly identifies as [10, Conjecture 4.7].
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the main content of the statement: it is about a smooth complex projective polarized variety (X,H), the existence of a class gamma in the numerical Chow ring of the form e^{-B}·(1,0,Gamma,gamma_3,...,gamma_n), an upper semicontinuous function f^gamma: R -> R, and a universal quadratic inequality Q_{s,q}(E) >= 0 for gamma-tilt-semistable objects in a region Delta. refined_question:
Let (X,H) be a smooth complex projective polarized variety of dimension n. Is it true that there exist classes B in NS(X) tensor R, Gamma in CH^2_num(X) tensor R with Gamma·H^{n-2} = 0, and gamma_i in CH^i_num(X) tensor R for 3 <= i <= n, defining

gamma := e^{-B}·(1,0,Gamma,gamma_3,...,gamma_n) in CH^bullet_num(X) tensor R,

and an upper semicontinuous function f^gamma: R -> R, such that for every (s,q) in Delta := {(s,q) in R^2 : q > s^2/2} and every object E in D^b(X) that is sigma^gamma_{s,q}-semistable, one has Q_{s,q}(E) >= 0 whenever q > f^gamma(s), where ch^gamma(-) := gamma·ch(-), v_H^gamma(E) := (H^n ch_0^gamma(E), H^{n-1} ch_1^gamma(E), ..., H·ch_{n-1}^gamma(E), ch_n^gamma(E)), and Q_{s,q}(E) is the Bayer–Macrì quadratic form built from the first four components v_0^gamma, v_1^gamma, v_2^gamma, v_3^gamma?
justification: The draft is aiming at the revised generalized Bogomolov–Gieseker conjecture stated in the survey as Conjecture 5.13, not at a different Torelli-type question. Section 5.3 first defines the ordinary tilt-stability family sigma_{s,q} and the parameter region Delta in Theorem 5.11, then explains why the older inequality is too optimistic, and finally introduces the modified class gamma, the modified Chern character ch^gamma, and the exact conjectural statement. The survey explicitly says that Conjecture 5.13 is [10, Conjecture 4.7], so this is the nearest official formulation in arXiv:2201.03899 itself. Your draft is mathematically close, but it omits several paper-critical definitions: the condition Gamma·H^{n-2}=0, the fact that semistability depends on the same pair (s,q), the definition of Delta, the ambient category D^b(X), and the auxiliary definitions needed to make Q_{s,q}(E) meaningful as a stand-alone question.

refined_question: Let X1 and X2 be cubic threefolds over an algebraically closed field K with char(K) != 2,3, and suppose there is an exact equivalence Ku(X1) ≅ Ku(X2). Can one prove X1 ≅ X2, i.e. reprove the categorical Torelli theorem for cubic threefolds (Theorem 6.4), by adapting the Section 4.1 extension method for Fourier-Mukai equivalences—through the semiorthogonal decompositions D^b(X_i) = <Ku(X_i), O_{X_i}, O_{X_i}(H_{X_i})>—so as to extend the equivalence from the Kuznetsov components to the whole derived categories and then apply the derived Torelli theorem for (anti)Fano manifolds?
justification: The nearest official formulation is not a conjecture in the introduction but the explicit open-ended Question 6.6 in Section 6.1. It asks verbatim whether Theorem 6.4 can be proved using the extension techniques from Section 4.1. This matches your draft almost exactly, except that the theorem and section numbers are off in your version. The paper's introduction also sets up precisely this contrast of methods: Enriques surfaces are treated by extending Fourier-Mukai equivalences (Section 4.1), whereas cubic threefolds are proved via stability conditions (Section 6.1). To make the question stand-alone and faithful, one must unpack Theorem 6.4, the cubic-threefold semiorthogonal decomposition, and the role of Proposition 4.1. The natural endgame of such an approach is to extend an equivalence Ku(X1) ≅ Ku(X2) to D^b(X1) ≅ D^b(X2), after which Theorem 3.2 would recover X1 ≅ X2 because cubic threefolds are Fano. Corollary 6.5 is also relevant context: it shows, as a consequence of Theorem 6.4, that Question 2.8 has a positive answer for cubic threefolds, highlighting exactly the Fourier-Mukai issue that a Section 4.1-style proof would need to confront independently.

Open Problems 1–2 supply the hidden scope that Open Problem 4 inherits: periodic boundary conditions for the time-dependent problem, and spatially non-constant steady states with zero-flux, homogeneous Neumann, or periodic boundary conditions for the steady problem. By contrast, Open Problems 6–7 concern a different system, namely the explicit mark-dynamics model (2.11), so they are not the closest match to your draft. Sect. 5.1.1 further explains why kernel regularity matters here: smooth kernels already permit well-posedness results for model (2.10), while the discontinuous top-hat case is analytically hardest. For suitable periodic initial data, in what function-space sense can one establish existence of time-dependent solutions to this explicit landscape-mark model (2.11), and does this solution theory remain well defined as R→0+, in the sense of yielding a meaningful local-limit connection to the system with p_i^{g,R} replaced by p_i? equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, one may pose the same existence/local-limit question for (2.11) on the d-dimensional torus, because the paper states that periodic boundary conditions in higher dimensions are equivalent to studying the problem on a torus. justification: The draft is already very close to Open Problem 6. Later discussion of boundary conditions explains that periodic boundary conditions are the analytically easiest case and are equivalent to working on a torus in higher dimensions; the well-posedness discussion also emphasizes that top-hat kernels are analytically difficult because of their discontinuity.

refined_question:
For the one-dimensional discrete-delay scalar model from Section 2.3.1, namely
u_t = D1 u_xx + D2 d/dx(u d/dx u(x,t-tau)) + f(u(x,t), ubar(t)) for x in Omega=(0,L), t>0,
where tau>0, D1>0, D2 is real, and ubar(t) = |Omega|^{-1} integral_Omega u(y,t) dy is the spatial average of the population over the whole domain, under what assumptions on the coefficients, the growth law f, and the prescribed initial/history data on Omega x [-tau,0] does the problem with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions u_x(0,t)=u_x(L,t)=0 admit a unique solution for t>0? In the same model, can analogous existence-and-uniqueness results be established on bounded domains in higher spatial dimensions or under other boundary conditions?
justification: The draft matches Open Problem 25 in Section 2.3.1 because the paper's first modification of the delayed advection model changes the growth term to depend on the spatial domain average, giving equation (2.21) with the averaged quantity ubar(t)=|Omega|^{-1} integral_Omega u(y,t) dy. The official open question attached to that model is exactly the existence/uniqueness problem under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, followed by the extensions to higher dimensions and other boundary conditions. Section 5.1.2 confirms that model (2.21) is the unresolved well-posedness case among the explicit-memory models and notes that its nonlocality is only in the reaction term, which helps pin down the intended scope. Section 4.1 supplies the paper's meaning of homogeneous Neumann boundary data as du/dn = 0 on the boundary.

Let Omega be a bounded domain in R^n, let tau,sigma > 0, let d be a real parameter and lambda > 0, and consider the delayed diffusion-advection equation
u_t = Delta u + d div(u grad u_tau) + lambda u F(u,u_sigma) in Omega for t > 0,

justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s Open Problem 26, which is posed immediately after the introduction of model (2.23) in the discrete-delay scalar section. It restores the paper’s exact PDE structure, including the two distinct delays, the nonlocal delayed term u_sigma, the role of the kernel K, the parameters d and lambda, and the fact that the boundary condition is homogeneous Dirichlet. It also incorporates the nearby contextual points the paper treats as part of well-posedness: uniqueness is relative to given initial data, one must specify a solution notion, and for time-dependent problems one should be explicit about whether existence is local or global. This is paper-faithful and sharper than the draft while staying as close as possible to the original open problem.

justification: The closest official statement is Open Problem 29 in Section 2.3.1. The paper first introduces the local discrete-delay scalar model (2.20) and then explicitly asks in Open Problem 24 how adding nonlocal perception with a top-hat detection function changes the dynamics. It next introduces the local delayed consumer-resource system (2.24), then states Open Problem 28 for the existence of the corresponding nonlocal-perception delayed extensions, and finally states Open Problem 29: in what sense may these problems converge as R -> 0+, and what are the qualitative differences between local and nonlocal time-delay problems. Section 2.1 supplies the precise top-hat kernel and the formal local-limit property lim_{R -> 0+} g_R = delta, while Section 5.3 identifies the purely local delayed models as the kernel choice g(x) = delta(x), G(t) = delta(t - tau). I therefore kept the question narrowly tied to models (2.20) and (2.24), added the missing kernel/domain/parameter notation from the nearby context, and preserved the paper’s deliberately open phrasing 'in what sense' rather than imposing a stronger convergence claim. I did not broaden the problem beyond these specific delayed movement formulations.

original_question: Let μ be a non-negative finite Borel measure on R^3 representing an extended nuclear charge distribution, with total charge μ(R^3) ≤ 1. Consider the Dirac-Coulomb operator D0 - μ * |x|^{-1}, where D0 is the free Dirac operator and μ * |x|^{-1} is the electrostatic potential generated by μ. Denote by λ1(D0 - μ * |x|^{-1}) the lowest eigenvalue of this operator in the spectral gap (-1, 1). Is this eigenvalue always minimized, among all such charge distributions with the same total charge, when the entire charge is concentrated at one point, so that λ1(D0 - μ * |x|^{-1}) ≥ λ1(D0 - μ(R^3)/|x|) = sqrt(1 - μ(R^3)^2)?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1: for each fixed total charge ν in [0,1], the first gap eigenvalue of the Dirac operator D0−μ*|x|^{-1} should be minimized by the point charge νδ0, so that λ1(D0−μ*|x|^{-1}) ≥ λ1(D0−ν/|x|)=√(1−ν^2). The chapter abstract and the opening of Section 34.1 identify exactly this as the main question. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-12244-6_34))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper’s central object and comparison almost exactly: a non-negative finite Borel measure μ on R^3, the electrostatic potential μ*|x|^{-1}, the Dirac operator D0, the first eigenvalue in the spectral gap, the fixed-total-charge comparison, and the special role of the fully concentrated point charge. This is precisely how the chapter frames the open problem. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-12244-6_34))

original_question: Let M ≥ 2 point nuclei with charges θ1, ..., θM ≥ 0 and positions R1, ..., RM in R^3 satisfy Σ_{m=1}^M θm ≤ 1. Is this eigenvalue always at least as large as the lowest gap eigenvalue for the single-center Coulomb field carrying the same total charge, namely does λ1(D0 - Σ_{m=1}^M θm/|x - Rm|) ≥ λ1(D0 - (Σ_{m=1}^M θm)/|x|) = sqrt(1 - (Σ_{m=1}^M θm)^2) hold for every choice of M, positions, and charges with total charge at most 1?

original_question: Let μ be a non-negative Borel measure on R^3 with total charge μ(R^3) ≤ 1, and let f: R^3 → R^3 be a contraction for the Euclidean norm. Write f_*μ for the pushforward of μ under f, so f_*μ represents a version of the same charge distribution moved closer together by the contraction. If λ1(D0 - ν * |x|^{-1}) denotes the lowest eigenvalue in the spectral gap (-1, 1) of the Dirac-Coulomb operator generated by a charge distribution ν, does every Euclidean contraction fail to increase this eigenvalue, i.e. does λ1(D0 - μ * |x|^{-1}) ≥ λ1(D0 - (f_*μ) * |x|^{-1}) always hold?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1, with Proposition 1.2 giving the equivalent contraction formulation that the draft is aiming at.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the ambient space R^3, uses a non-negative Borel charge distribution μ, introduces pushforward under a Euclidean contraction, and asks about monotonicity of the first gap eigenvalue of a Dirac–Coulomb operator when the charge is made more concentrated. refined_question: Let D0 = -iα·∇ + β on L^2(R^3, C^4), in units m = c = ħ = 1, and let λ1(D0 - μ * |x|^{-1}) denote the first eigenvalue in the spectral gap (-1,1) of the distinguished self-adjoint Dirac operator with Coulomb potential generated by a non-negative finite Borel measure μ on R^3. target_in_paper: Problem 4 in Section 3.1 ("Variational Setting for Shocks"): the question of extending Arnold’s geodesic framework from the diffeomorphism group D(M) to the semigroup Map(M) so as to capture smooth solutions and their continuations beyond shock formation for Burgers-like and compressible fluid equations.

refined_question: Let M be a manifold of arbitrary dimension. The inviscid Burgers equation ∂_t v + v·∇v = 0 can be viewed as a geodesic equation on the full diffeomorphism group D(M) endowed with a non-invariant L^2 metric, but once shock waves form the Lagrangian evolution no longer remains in D(M). Can one formulate an extension of Arnold’s geodesic/variational framework from D(M) to the semigroup Map(M) of self-maps of M—possibly in a Lipschitz class—so that it describes particle trajectories both before and after shock formation, recovers the pre-shock non-invariant L^2 geodesic description, and is compatible after collision with the Bogaevsky "circle law" for potential solutions with convex potentials, thereby capturing smooth solutions and their continuations beyond emergence of shock waves for Burgers-like and compressible fluid equations?
justification: This is the exact official problem your draft is aiming at: Problem 4 in Section 3.1 repeats the D(M) to Map(M) extension almost verbatim. The nearby context in the same section supplies the hidden scope and assumptions that make the question stand alone: Burgers is viewed as a geodesic equation on D(M) with a non-invariant L^2 metric; shocks break the D(M)-evolution; the desired extension should be a variational principle on maps M to itself, possibly Lipschitz, valid both before and after shock formation, and consistent with the pre-shock geodesic picture and the post-collision circle law. I did not replace it by Problem 5, because Problem 5 is a broader neighboring question about multidimensional sticking particles and both potential and non-potential flows.

justification: The draft is targeting Section 3.2, Problem 5, not the broader Section 3.1, Problem 4. Problem 5 states almost exactly what the draft asks. The surrounding discussion fixes the intended scope: Section 3.2 first constructs a variational principle in one dimension by enlarging the configuration space and minimizing the action for finite and continuous families of sticking particles; then Remark 3.2 explains why the multidimensional case is genuinely open, namely because admissible configurations are no longer convex, collisions are harder to parametrize, and shock hypersurfaces with concentrated mass are difficult to capture variationally. Problem 4 is related but broader, since it asks for an extension of Arnold's geodesic framework to a semigroup of maps for Burgers-like and compressible equations, so it should not replace the narrower and more exact Problem 5.

For a probability measure μ on X and parameter δ, define H_{ε,δ}(μ)=inf{H_ε(Y): Y⊂X is compact and μ(X\Y)≤δ}. Now assume X is a Hilbert space with chosen coordinates x_1,x_2,..., let X_n={x_i=0 for i>n}, let π_n:X→X_n be the orthogonal projection, partition X_n into ε-cubes C_j, and write K_j=π_n^{-1}(C_j). refined_question: Under PAC learning of Boolean functions over {0,1}^n under the uniform distribution with membership queries, let f:{0,1}^n→{0,1} be an unknown size-s decision tree. original_question: Given a projective variety X with mild singularities and a maximal rationally connected (MRC) fibration phi: X -> Y defined only up to birational modification of the base, under what assumptions can one choose a birational model of Y so that the MRC fibration is represented by a holomorphic morphism rather than merely an almost holomorphic rational map?

refined_question: Let X be a complex projective variety with mild singularities (for example, klt singularities), and let ψ: X ⇢ Y be a maximal rationally connected fibration, i.e. an almost holomorphic rational map to a projective variety Y whose general fibers are rationally connected and such that no horizontal rational curve passes through a very general point of X. Since the base Y is only defined up to birational equivalence and may be replaced by a smooth birational model, when can one choose this birational model so that ψ is represented by a holomorphic morphism X → Y rather than only by an almost holomorphic rational map?

original_question: If a compact Kahler manifold X has positive holomorphic sectional curvature, must X be projective and rationally connected?
target_in_paper: Section 3, Conjecture 3.1 (Yau’s conjecture): if a compact Kähler manifold X has positive holomorphic sectional curvature, then X is projective and rationally connected.
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s intended target almost verbatim: it has the correct ambient object (a compact Kähler manifold X), the correct hypothesis (positive holomorphic sectional curvature), and the exact two conclusions stated in the paper (projective and rationally connected).

Problem 3.3 and Theorem 3.4 are nearby context about the semi-positive case and structure results, but they are not closer matches to the draft than Conjecture 3.1 itself.

The decisive clues are the orbifold morphism, the boundary on the base pair, the slope rationally connected general orbifold fibers, and the local triviality with respect to pairs: these are exactly the three bullet points of Conjecture 5.4. The nearby paragraph explicitly says that ordinary MRC fibrations forget the boundary Delta and that the slope rationally connected quotient is the boundary-sensitive replacement; it then introduces Conjecture 5.4 as the sought structure theorem for that quotient. refined_question: Let mu=(mu_1,mu_2) be a two-armed Bernoulli bandit instance in S with a unique best arm I*(mu). A fixed-budget algorithm sequentially chooses arms based on past observations and, after exactly n samples, outputs a recommendation hat I_n; write p_{mu,n}=P_mu(hat I_n != I*(mu)). In the nearby non-adaptive large-deviations formulation, the oracle sampling proportion w*(mu) in Sigma_2 achieves Gamma_na^*(mu)=sup_{w in Sigma_2} inf_{nu in Alt(mu)} [w_1 KL(nu_1||mu_1)+w_2 KL(nu_2||mu_2)]^{-1}, but w*(mu) depends on the unknown Bernoulli means and so cannot be fixed a priori. Does there exist an adaptive fixed-budget algorithm that does not know mu_1 or mu_2 in advance and nevertheless, for every such two-armed Bernoulli instance mu, satisfies limsup_{n->infinity} n/log(1/p_{mu,n}) <= Gamma_na^*(mu), i.e. achieves the same asymptotically optimal fixed-budget performance as the oracle rule based on w*(mu)?
justification: The draft is not really aiming at Open problem 1 or Open problem 2, both of which are broader. Its nearest match is the informal Bernoulli-specific question closing Section 5. The paper first defines the fixed-budget criterion p_{mu,n} and the general notion of asymptotic fixed-budget complexity, then in Section 4 introduces the non-adaptive complexity Gamma_na^*(mu) and the oracle optimizer w*(mu), explicitly noting that w*(mu) depends on the unknown instance and is therefore not a valid adaptive rule. Section 5 then specializes this exact obstruction to two-armed Bernoulli bandits and says it is unclear whether one can still achieve asymptotic optimality without that oracle requirement. The refined question therefore makes the loss, quantifiers, asymptotic criterion, and oracle benchmark explicit while staying as narrow as the paper itself.

justification: The draft is trying to capture Open Problem 4.1 in Section 4. Let d,n\in \mathbb N, and let D_d\subset \mathbb R^d be an open set with Lebesgue measure \lambda_d(D_d)=1. Define
\widetilde C^2(D_d):=\{f\in C^2(D_d;\mathbb R): \|f\|_\infty\le 1,\ \operatorname{Lip}(f)\le d^{-1/2},\ \operatorname{Lip}(D^\Theta f)\le d^{-1}\ \text{for every }\Theta\in S^{d-1}\},
where D^\Theta f denotes the directional derivative in direction \Theta and \operatorname{Lip}(g):=\sup_{x,y\in D_d,\ x\ne y}|g(x)-g(y)|/\|x-y\|_2. Let e(n,\widetilde C^2(D_d)) be the minimal worst-case error of deterministic algorithms that approximate \int_{D_d} f(x)\,dx using n function values. Is it true that there exists a constant C>0, independent of both d and D_d, such that
 e(n,\widetilde C^2(D_d))\ge C\,n^{-2/d}
for all d,n\in \mathbb N and all such domains D_d?
justification: The draft is targeting Example 1 in Section 4, not one of the paper’s earlier lower-bound statements for the non-rotationally-invariant classes F_d^k(D_d). The introduction supplies the meaning of e(n,F_d) as the optimal deterministic worst-case integration error based on n function values. Is it true that for every such f, the algebra M(f) has the weak Lefschetz property, i.e. there exists a linear form L\in M(f)_1 such that \times L\colon M(f)_i\to M(f)_{i+1} has maximal rank for all i? More strongly, must M(f) always have the strong Lefschetz property, i.e. does there exist L\in M(f)_1 such that \times L^m\colon M(f)_i\to M(f)_{i+m} has maximal rank for all i and all m\ge 1?
justification: The draft does not target any Conjecture 1.1/Proposition 1.2/Theorem 1.3 in this paper, because arXiv:2311.03081 is a problem list and the matching item is instead Section 2, Question 2.8. Section 2 first sets the standing assumption of characteristic zero, and the Jacobian-ideals paragraph then specializes to S=\mathbb{C}[x_0,\dots,x_n], homogeneous f of degree d, smooth V(f)\subset \mathbb{P}^n, J_f generated by the partial derivatives, and M(f)=S/J_f. The official formulation is exactly: whether M(f) has the WLP (or the SLP) for any homogeneous form f with smooth V(f). The same paragraph supplies the paper-specific scope and motivation: generic f is known to give both WLP and SLP, and WLP is already known for f\in \mathbb{C}[x_0,\dots,x_3] of degree d\le 6 with smooth V(f).

Must there exist an integer k >= 0 and constants c, C > 0 such that c n^k <= deg(f^n) <= C n^k for all sufficiently large n? Moreover, if k >= 1, must f preserve a rational fibration, i.e. is there a nonconstant dominant rational map pi: C^d -> B with 0 < dim(B) < d and a birational self-map g: B -> B such that pi o f = g o pi?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 10.1, Question 39, not a broader neighboring problem. The match is direct: the paper asks whether a polynomial automorphism f of C^d with lambda(f)=1 must satisfy deg(f^n) ~ n^k for some k in N, and whether the case k >= 1 forces preservation of a rational fibration (Section 10.1, Question 39, p. 23). The nearby context that must be imported for a stand-alone formulation is: (i) the higher-dimensional scope inherited from Problem 8, namely d >= 3 (Section 10.1, Problem 8, p. 23); (ii) the definition of lambda(f) via the limit of deg(f^n)^(1/n), established from submultiplicativity in the paragraph immediately preceding Question 39 (Section 10.1, p. 23); and (iii) the degree notation referenced back to Section 6.1 (Section 6.1, p. 14; Section 10.1, p. 23). The paragraph after Question 39 explicitly says that Question 40 is a weaker form of the same problem, so there is no paper-proved equivalent reformulation to supply (Section 10.1, Question 40, p. 23).

refined_question: Let C : f = 0 ⊂ P^2_C be a non-free arrangement of d >= 4 distinct lines, with f in S = C[x,y,z] homogeneous, and let r = mdr(f) >= 2 be the minimal degree of a nonzero homogeneous Jacobian relation a f_x + b f_y + c f_z = 0. If m(C) denotes the maximal multiplicity of a point of C and n(C) denotes the maximal multiplicity of a point of C \ {p}, where p is a point of multiplicity m(C), then the general lower bound tau(C) >= tau(d,r)_min := (d-1)(d-r-1) is known not to be optimal for line arrangements, while Theorem 6.2 and Corollary 6.3 give the stronger bounds tau(C) >= tau(d,r)_min + binom(r,2) + binom(n(C),2) + 1 and, when r != d - m(C), tau(C) >= tau(d,r)_min + binom(r,2) + binom(m(C),2) + 1, hence in particular tau(C) >= tau(d,r)_min + binom(r,2) + 4 when r >= 3 and n(C) >= 3. equivalent_formulation: Equivalent formulation (using formula (6.3) from the paper): determine the optimal lower bound, under the same hypotheses, for mu(C) = sum_p (n(p)-1)^2, since for line arrangements one has tau(C) = mu(C).
justification: The draft is clearly targeting the part of Section 6 dealing with minimal, not maximal, Tjurina numbers. The paper first recalls the general du Plessis-Wall lower bound tau(d,r)_min in Theorem 2.4, then explains that this lower bound is effective for general reduced plane curves but is not optimal for line arrangements. It next states the sharper line-arrangement bounds in Theorem 6.2 and Corollary 6.3, using the invariants r = mdr(f), m(C), and n(C), and then ends that discussion with the explicit open problem of finding the best lower bound for the global Tjurina number of line arrangements. So the closest paper-faithful sharpening of your draft is not a broad question about arbitrary auxiliary invariants, but this specific Section 6 open problem, stated with the precise notation and hypotheses supplied there.

original_question: Do the classes MSJ(2) and MSJ(3) coincide for measure-preserving Z-actions? Here T belongs to MSJ(n) if every ergodic self-joining of n copies of T, other than the product measure mu^{otimes n}, has at least one projection to a two-dimensional face of X x ... x X equal to Delta_{T^i}, the image of the diagonal measure under a power T^i.

correct_elements: Your draft identifies the right problem in the paper: the MSJ(2) versus MSJ(3) question for measure-preserving Z-actions generated by a single transformation T. refined_question: Let T be an ergodic invertible measure-preserving transformation of a standard Lebesgue probability space (X, B, μ). correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the two linked assertions discussed around positive local rank: (i) existence of a measure-preserving automorphism with absolutely continuous spectrum of finite multiplicity, and (ii) the possibility that every mixing automorphism of positive local rank is mixing of all orders. refined_question: Let I_2(T)=∫_0^T |ζ(1/2+it)|^4 dt, where ζ(s) is the Riemann zeta function. Prove a stronger error term by showing that there exists θ<2/3 such that I_2(T)=T P_4(log T)+O(T^(θ+ε)) for every ε>0. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))

Assuming the Riemann Hypothesis, let m ≥ 1 be fixed, let k = (k_1, …, k_m) with k_i > 0, and let α = (α_1, …, α_m) where each α_i = α_i(T) is a real-valued function satisfying α_i = o(T), such that each limit lim_{T→∞} α_i log T and each limit lim_{T→∞}(α_i − α_j) log T exists in ℝ ∪ {±∞}, and for i ≠ j one has α_i ≠ α_j and α_i − α_j = O(1). Define
M_k(T, α) = ∫_0^T ∏_{i=1}^m |ζ(1/2 + i(t + α_i))|^(2k_i) dt.
Use Harper’s method to prove that, for all sufficiently large T,
M_k(T, α) ≪_k T (log T)^(k_1^2 + ··· + k_m^2) ∏_{1≤i<j≤m} (min{1/|α_i − α_j|, log T})^(2k_i k_j),
thereby removing the ε from Chandee’s quoted bound while keeping the same hypotheses on the shifts. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))

original_question: Characterize the Krylov intersection and Krylov reducibility for Friedrichs operators. In the bounded setting, the Krylov intersection is I(A, g) = K(A, g) ∩ A(K(A, g)^⊥); in the unbounded setting, when the Krylov subspace is defined, the corresponding expression is I(A, g) = K(A, g) ∩ A(K(A, g)^⊥ ∩ dom A). Krylov reducibility asks whether K(A, g)^⊥ is also invariant under A, equivalently whether A K(A, g)^⊥ ⊂ K(A, g)^⊥. The problem is to determine these structures both for abstract Friedrichs operators on Hilbert space and, concretely, for the classical Friedrichs differential operator.

original_question: Consider gradient descent on a convex function f: R^d -> R that is L-smooth, meaning that its gradient exists and is L-Lipschitz. original_question: In a quasi-Banach space, does the equivalence between almost-greedy bases and semi-greedy bases remain true for general Markushevich bases, without assuming that the basis is Schauder? Here, almost-greedy means that greedy projections approximate as well as the best coordinate projections up to a uniform constant, while semi-greedy means that for each greedy set A, the best approximation inside span{x_n : n in A} is bounded by a constant times the best |A|-term approximation error.

correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper's actual target: the quasi-Banach-space extension of the Banach-space equivalence between almost-greedy and semi-greedy Markushevich bases, specifically asking whether one can drop the Schauder-basis hypothesis. original_question: Let Ω be a Polish space. We call a semigroup T = (T (t))t≥0 of contractions on Cb (Ω) a transition semigroup if (i) for every f ∈ Cb (E) we have T (t)f → T (s)f locally uniformly whenever t → s and (ii) for every t ≥ 0 and every uniformly bounded sequence (fn )n∈N ⊂ Cb (Ω) that converges locally uniformly to f , we have that T (t)fn converges locally uniformly to f . Is there a characterization of the generators of such a semigroup akin to the Lumer–Phillips theorem?
target_in_paper: Section 1, Problem 3 (“Lumer–Phillips for transition semigroups”).
correct_elements: The draft already captures the correct open problem very closely: it has the right ambient setting (a Polish space Ω), the right function space C_b(Ω), the two continuity/compatibility conditions used to define the paper’s transition semigroups, and the correct goal of seeking a Lumer–Phillips-type generation theorem.

refined_question: Let Ω be a Polish space, and let C_b(Ω) be the Banach space of bounded continuous scalar-valued functions on Ω with the supremum norm. Call a semigroup T = (T(t))_{t ≥ 0} on C_b(Ω) a contraction transition semigroup if ||T(t)|| ≤ 1 for all t ≥ 0, if for every f ∈ C_b(Ω) one has T(t)f → T(s)f locally uniformly on Ω whenever t → s, and if for every t ≥ 0 and every uniformly bounded sequence (f_n) ⊂ C_b(Ω) with f_n → f locally uniformly on Ω, one has T(t)f_n → T(t)f locally uniformly on Ω. Can one formulate a usable Lumer–Phillips-type generation theorem for this class—preferably in terms analogous to dissipativity plus a range condition, and avoiding Hille–Yosida resolvent-power bounds—that characterizes, or at least gives practically verifiable sufficient conditions for, when a linear operator A on C_b(Ω) generates such a contraction transition semigroup? In the spirit of the paper, additional assumptions natural in applications, such as positivity of the resolvent or a strong Feller property of the resolvent, may be allowed.

The comments also state that usability is the priority and that even a sufficient criterion, possibly using positivity or strong Feller assumptions on the resolvent, would already be valuable. I also normalized the notation to C_b(Ω), made the norm and topology explicit, and wrote condition (ii) in the natural continuity form needed for a self-contained formulation.

refined_question: Let X=UC_b(R,\mathbb{R}) be the Banach space of bounded uniformly continuous real-valued functions on \mathbb{R}, with the supremum norm, and let D_0 be the dense subspace of all bounded C^\infty-functions on \mathbb{R} whose derivatives of every order are bounded. Let a,b,c\in X be arbitrary real-valued functions with a(x)\ge a_0>0 for all x\in\mathbb{R}, and define on D_0 the differential operator (Lf)(x)=a(x)f''(x)+b(x)f'(x)+c(x)f(x). It is known that the closure \overline{L} generates a C_0-semigroup (e^{t\overline{L}})_{t\ge 0} on X. correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's target almost exactly: it uses two Coxeter systems, assumes the two Bruhat intervals are isomorphic as posets, and asks whether the ordinary Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials are equal. If [u,v] and [w,z] are isomorphic as posets, must the ordinary Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials of the two intervals coincide, i.e. must P_{u,v}(q) = P_{w,z}(q) in Z[q]?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, under the same hypotheses, must the ordinary R-polynomials agree: R_{u,v}(q) = R_{w,z}(q)?
justification: The draft is essentially Conjecture 1.4 verbatim. In Section 1 the paper first defines the ordinary Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials by specializing the parabolic family in Theorem 1.3, with P_{u,v} = P^{∅,-1}_{u,v} (= P^{∅,q}_{u,v}), and similarly defines the ordinary R-polynomials from Theorem 1.2. It then states Conjecture 1.4 exactly for isomorphic Bruhat intervals as posets. The paragraph immediately following Conjecture 1.4 says that replacing the equality of Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials by the equality of R-polynomials gives an equivalent conjecture. So the only real improvements needed are to spell out Bruhat order, the meaning of interval notation, the ordinary/non-parabolic meaning of P_{u,v}, and the universal quantifiers. No extra hypotheses about type, field, characteristic, homogeneity, or degree restrictions belong to the conjecture itself.

Define the Gram map G: Sym_{k+1}(R) → F_{n+1,2d} by A ↦ f_A(X) = q_A(m_0(X),...,m_k(X)), where q_A(Z) = Z^t A Z. For i = 0,...,k−n, let H_i = {[z] ∈ P^k | there exists x ∈ C^{n+1} with (z_0,...,z_{n+i}) = (m_0(x),...,m_{n+i}(x))}, let V_i ⊆ P^k be the Zariski closure of H_i, and let C_i = {f ∈ F_{n+1,2d} | there exists A ∈ G^{-1}(f) such that q_A is nonnegative on V_i(R)}. justification: The nearest official formulation is Open problem 3 in Section 2, whose wording is essentially: is it possible to construct a counterexample to the Ball-Evans approximation problem for some p ≥ [n/2] in higher dimensions? This is exactly the issue your draft is aiming at. To make it stand-alone and paper-faithful, one has to restore the ambient Sobolev setting f ∈ W^{1,p}(Ω, R^n), the existential quantifiers over n, p, Ω, and f, and the fact that the approximation is in the strong W^{1,p} norm. Theorem 2.2 and the paragraph immediately after it explain the sharp nearby context: counterexamples are known for n ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ p < ⌊n/2⌋ by using homeomorphisms whose Jacobian changes sign, while for p > ⌊n/2⌋ that sign-changing mechanism is unavailable because Jacobians of Sobolev homeomorphisms cannot change sign. That is why Open problem 3 asks whether a different counterexample may still exist for some p ≥ ⌊n/2⌋. Finally, the paper also stresses in Open problem 2 that, in dimensions n ≥ 3, approximation by diffeomorphisms and by piecewise affine homeomorphisms should not be silently treated as already equivalent.

refined_question: In the topos SymSet = PSh(F) of symmetric simplicial sets, where F is the category of non-empty finite sets and all maps, the levels are indexed by the total order -infinity < 0 < 1 < 2 < ... < infinity, with level l induced by the inclusion of the full subcategory F_l on sets of cardinality at most l+1. For each level l, let a_l be the least level m such that every l-skeletal symmetric set is m-coskeletal. Here l-skeletal means that the counit sk_l X -> X is an isomorphism (equivalently, every structure in X has mass at most l+1), and m-coskeletal means that the unit X -> cosk_m X is an isomorphism (equivalently, every k-cycle with k > m has a unique filler). Determine the exact Aufhebung function l |-> a_l for PSh(F), and hence the precise way-above relation between levels in combinatorial terms.
equivalent_formulation: Because the levels form a total order and a_l is defined as the least level way above l, this is equivalent to classifying all pairs (l, m) such that every l-skeletal symmetric set is m-coskeletal, namely those with m >= a_l.

Establish or refute the following conjecture for the discrete minimal Riesz 2-energy on the unit sphere S^2 ⊂ R^3 with respect to the Euclidean distance: if
E_2(S^2; N) := min_{x_1,...,x_N ∈ S^2} Σ_{i≠j} 1/||x_i - x_j||^2,
then, as N → ∞,
E_2(S^2; N) = (1/4) N^2 log N + C_{2,2} N^2 + o(N^2),
where
C_{2,2} = (1/4)(γ - log(2√(3π))) + (√3/(4π))(γ_1(2/3) - γ_1(1/3)),
and γ_1(a) denotes the generalized Stieltjes constant appearing in the Laurent expansion of the Hurwitz zeta function ζ(s,a) at s = 1.

refined_question: For integers n≥1 and 0≤m≤n, let T be a rooted labelled tree of size n on [n], and let f:[n]→[n] be an n-mapping. original_question: Let X_1 follow a Laplace distribution with mean 0 and scale 1/sqrt(2), let X_2 follow a t distribution with 5 degrees of freedom, location 0, and scale sqrt(3/5), and let X_1 and X_2 be independent. correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact distributions used in Example 3, the normalization α^2 + β^2 = 1, the independence of X1 and X2, the intended conclusion 'identifiable up to signs', and the key obstruction that the fourth-moment criterion from Theorem 6 does not certify that conclusion in the numerically problematic regime |α| ≥ 0.1835. justification: The draft captures the motivating sentence in Section 2, but the paper's actual open problem is sharper and more specific. Section 2 first states that a random 4-regular graph G formed from two uniformly random cycles is a.a.s. 3-colorable and asks whether it is also a.a.s. 3-choosable. It then introduces the Alon-Tarsi method in Theorem 2.1, defines the graph polynomial P_G, observes that in the 4-regular case the only relevant monomial is ∏ v^2, and finally states the official open problem as Problem 2.1 asking whether the coefficient of that monomial is a.a.s. non-zero. So the paper-faithful stand-alone question should be the coefficient non-vanishing problem, not the broader motivational paraphrase about 3-choosability. The footnote to Section 2 also clarifies the random model and its relation to simple uniformly random 4-regular graphs.

original_question: Let G = (V, E) be a directed graph, let A be a non-trivial Abelian group, and let f map E into A. A snark is a cubic non-3-edge-colorable cyclically 4-edge-connected graph with girth at least 5, and it is bicritical if removing any two distinct vertices produces a 3-edge-colorable graph. refined_question: Let P = P[ρ,a_1,...,a_{d-2}] be the Poisson bivector on the affine space R^d corresponding to the Nambu-determinant bracket {f,g}_d(x) = ρ(x) det(∂(f,g,a_1,...,a_{d-2})/∂(x^1,...,x^d)), where f, g, a_i ∈ C^1(R^d) and the a_i are Casimirs. Assuming, as in the paper’s higher-dimensional setting, that Kontsevich’s tetrahedral cocycle γ3 restricts to this Nambu subset for d > 3, does the induced infinitesimal deformation Ṗ = Q_{γ3}(P^{⊗4}) become genuinely nontrivial in the unresolved higher-dimensional cases, or is it always infinitesimally trivial, i.e. generated by a coordinate change along some dimension-dependent vector field X_d^{γ3}(P^{⊗3}) on R^d satisfying Q_{γ3}(P^{⊗4}) = [[P, X_d^{γ3}(P^{⊗3})]]?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent formulation: for the associated Poisson bivector P, is the tetrahedral infinitesimal deformation a Poisson coboundary, namely Q_{γ3}(P^{⊗4}) = [[P, X_d^{γ3}(P^{⊗3})]] for some vector field X_d^{γ3} on R^d, or not?
justification: The draft is aiming at the introduction’s exact 'standard problem in deformation theory': whether the tetrahedral γ3-flow on the Nambu-determinant brackets is nontrivial or merely a coordinate change (§1, pp. 90–91). Page 93 makes the same issue precise in the bivector language Ṗ = Q_{γ3}(P^{⊗4}) and the coboundary criterion Q_{γ3} = [[P, X^{γ3}]], so this is the nearest official formulation of your draft. The final paragraph on p. 95 shows that the paper now treats the open higher-dimensional Nambu cases as the live scope, while Proposition 1 on p. 94 is nearby technical context about the d ↦ d + 1 reduction and not itself the main nontriviality question. I therefore kept the question narrow: the tetrahedral γ3-flow, the specific Nambu-determinant brackets (1), the affine space R^d, and the precise coordinate-change/coboundary notion of triviality.

justification: The wording of your draft matches the second bullet in the paper’s final open-problems list much more closely than Proposition 1 itself. The paper first sets up the Nambu-determinant bracket and the general triviality question for the tetrahedral cocycle action in Section 1. It then defines Nambu micro-graphs, descendants, and embeddings in Section 2, and explains that the trivializing 1-vectors are sought among micro-graphs with one sink and three Nambu blocks. Proposition 1 proves a special d=3 to 4 descendant-closure statement for vanishing descendants of the sunflower, namely that no extra vanishing 4D descendants need be sought outside descendants of the relevant 3D vanishing set. The final bullet list on page 95 then asks, in general, whether once one works inside 2D sunflower descendants, the search for X_{gamma_3}^{d+1} can be restricted to the union of descendants of X_{gamma_3}^d and descendants of vanishing 1-vector micro-graphs over R^d. That is exactly the paper-faithful sharpened version of your draft.

original_question: Within the class of tiling billiards in periodic tilings, is there a finite list of generic archetypal behaviors? refined_question:
Let X be a smooth complex projective curve (compact Riemann surface) of genus g >= 2, let SU_X(r) be the moduli space of semistable rank-r vector bundles on X with trivial determinant, and let L_X be its determinant line bundle. For each integer k >= 1, Theorem 7 states that, as X varies in the moduli stack M_g of smooth genus-g curves, the linear systems |L_X^k| form a flat projective bundle. Hence one obtains a projective monodromy representation
ρ_{r,k}: Γ_g = π_1(M_g, X) -> PGL(H^0(SU_X(r), L_X^k)).
What is this projective representation ρ_{r,k}?
justification: The draft is already very close to the paper's exact target. In Section 9, Beauville first states in Theorem 7 that the linear systems |L_t^k| attached to a family of smooth curves define a flat projective bundle; he then specializes to the moduli space M_g and says that this yields a projective representation ρ_{r,k} of Γ_g, followed immediately by Question 7: "What is the representation ρ_{r,k}?" The surrounding remarks explain the intended level of specificity: in rank one the corresponding action is classically described via theta-transformation formulas and factors through Sp(2g, Z), while for arbitrary rank Beauville notes that Theorem 2 gives an analogous description only in the special case k = 1, and he expects the general case to be more complicated. correct_elements: Your draft correctly isolates the paper’s contractible-surface setting, uses the standard exhaustion by large Euclidean sublevel sets coming from a proper algebraic embedding, and focuses on the intended obstruction: whether a nontrivial smooth contractible algebraic surface can have large strictly pseudoconvex contractible pieces that are holomorphically indistinguishable from domains in C^2.

refined_question: Let X be a smooth affine contractible algebraic surface over C with X not isomorphic to A^2_C. Fix a proper algebraic embedding X into C^N, let rho = ||.||^2|_X, and for all sufficiently large R let X_R = {x in X : rho(x) < R^2}; then X_R is a contractible strictly pseudoconvex domain in X with smooth real-algebraic boundary. Must it be true that, for every sufficiently large R, X_R is not biholomorphic to any domain in C^2?
justification: The draft is close in spirit, but it is slightly narrower than the paper’s actual intent. The accessible evidence around Zaidenberg’s Problem 5 shows that the core issue is whether exotic smooth contractible affine surfaces (i.e. smooth contractible affine surfaces over C not isomorphic to A^2_C) can be holomorphically realized in C^2, and the large strictly pseudoconvex exhaustion domains X_R are the standard concrete test objects used to sharpen that question. The main adjustment is therefore to replace 'bounded strictly pseudoconvex domain in C^2' by the paper-faithful 'domain in C^2'. I am also making explicit the affine/C-structure, the proper algebraic embedding, and the quantifier 'for every sufficiently large R'. Because the indexed sources available here expose the paper metadata and later quotations of Zaidenberg’s Problem 5 but not a fully searchable line-by-line OCR of the original 23-page preprint, the page pinpointing below is conservative.

original_question: Let X be a smooth Q-acyclic surface of log-general type, and let (V, D) be a minimal SNC-completion with X = V - D, where V is smooth projective and D is a simple normal crossings divisor. Must K_V (K_V + D) = 0, equivalently, since D is a rational tree, must the logarithmic Chern number c_1^2(X) = (K_V + D)^2 equal -2?

Your draft captures only its numerical consequence K_V·(K_V + D)=0 (equivalently 3c_2(X)-c_1^2(X)=5, hence c_1^2(X)=-2 for a Q-acyclic surface), not the full conjecture that X is rigid and unobstructed.

refined_question: Let X be a smooth complex Q-acyclic affine surface of log-general type, and let (V,D) be a minimal smooth projective completion with D a simple normal crossings divisor and X = V \ D. Is X rigid and are the infinitesimal deformations of the pair (V,D) unobstructed? In particular, must one have chi(Theta_V⟨D⟩) = K_V·(K_V + D) = 0; equivalently, 3c_2(X) - c_1^2(X) = 5, where c_1^2(X) = (K_V + D)^2?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, for such X and (V,D), must 3c_2(X) - c_1^2(X) = 5? Since X is Q-acyclic, c_2(X)=e(X)=1, so this is the same as c_1^2(X) = -2.
justification: arXiv:alg-geom/9506006 is an open-problems paper rather than a theorem/proposition paper, and the accessible indexing for that 1995 preprint does not expose a numbered statement matching your draft verbatim. The nearest official formulation traced back to that paper is Zaidenberg's later restatement of the same problem as Rigidity Conjecture I: every smooth Q-acyclic surface of log-general type is rigid and unobstructed; in particular, for a minimal smooth SNC-completion (V,D), chi(Theta_V⟨D⟩)=K_V·(K_V+D)=0, equivalently 3c_2(X)-c_1^2(X)=5. Your draft therefore isolates a correct numerical consequence of the conjecture, but it is not fully paper-faithful because it omits the main rigidity/unobstructedness assertion and the precise deformation-theoretic notation. The contextual definition of 'rigid/unobstructed' via the pair (V,D) is supplied in the introduction of Flenner-Zaidenberg's paper on rational cuspidal curves, which explicitly recalls the conjecture in this form.

justification: alg-geom/9506006 is not a theorem/proposition paper with a Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3; it is a conference problem list. So the right reconstruction has to come from the nearby contractible-variety/exotic-affine-space context rather than from nonexistent numbered results in that paper. The surrounding literature shows the exact tension your draft is trying to capture: Zaidenberg had already constructed countably many smooth contractible affine surfaces of hyperbolic/log-general type and used them to produce exotic affine structures on \mathbb{C}^n for n\ge 3, but those examples are products, not hypersurfaces, and in fact do not admit injective regular maps from \mathbb{C}^{n-1}. Kraft's survey, written at essentially the same moment, records that all smooth contractible surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 1 can be realized as hypersurfaces in \mathbb{A}^3, while infinitely many log-general-type contractible surfaces were also known. Kaliman-Makar-Limanov's C^4 hypersurface paper then makes clear that smooth contractible hypersurfaces in higher ambient dimension were being studied precisely in this period, and that some such hypersurfaces had only nonnegative logarithmic Kodaira dimension. Put together, the nearest sharp paper-faithful formulation is the higher-dimensional hypersurface existence question with maximal logarithmic Kodaira dimension, stated using \bar\kappa(X)=n-1 rather than the looser phrase in the draft. refined_question: Let X be a finite single-particle state space, let w={w_x}_{x in X} be complex fugacities, and let W:X x X -> C be a symmetric two-particle Boltzmann factor. original_question: Given n points in space with no four coplanar, determine the largest integer m for which one can guarantee that some m of the n points are the vertices of a convex polyhedron.
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in Section 1, specialized to d = 3, together with the introductory definition of ES_d(n), general position, and convex position.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the 3-dimensional setting, the general-position condition in that setting ('no four coplanar'), and the target configuration as a subset that forms the vertex set of a convex polyhedron.

refined_question: For each integer t >= 1, let ES_3(t) denote the smallest integer N such that every set of N points in Euclidean 3-space R^3 in general position (that is, with no four points coplanar) contains a t-point subset in convex position, equivalently, t points that are the vertices of a convex polyhedron. Is it true that ES_3(t) = 2^{Theta(sqrt(t))} as t -> infinity?
justification: The supplied identifier math/0010143 resolves on arXiv to an unrelated number-theory paper, 'Thirty-Six Unsolved Problems in Number Theory', whereas your draft and your instruction to prioritize Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, and Theorem 1.3 match Mubayi-Suk, 'The Erdős-Szekeres problem and an induced Ramsey question.' ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0010143)) In that paper, the geometric object is the higher-dimensional Erdős-Szekeres threshold ES_d(n): the minimum number of points in R^d in general position needed to force an n-point subset in convex position; Conjecture 1.1 predicts ES_d(n) = 2^{Theta(n^{1/(d-1)})} for every d >= 3. Specializing to d = 3 gives exactly the sharp, stand-alone question above. Proposition 1.2 provides the induced-hypergraph reformulation via Motzkin's 0/2/4 phenomenon, and Theorem 1.3 supplies evidence by proving a strong lower bound for the associated induced Ramsey number. correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official formulation essentially verbatim: k is fixed and positive; the equation is x^p - y^q = k; the variables x, y, p, q are all integers at least 2; and the claim is that there are only finitely many solution quadruples.
refined_question: For a fixed positive integer k, does the exponential Diophantine equation x^p - y^q = k have only finitely many solutions in integers x, y, p, q with x, y, p, q >= 2?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, in the increasing sequence of perfect powers x^p with x >= 2 and p >= 2, do the differences between consecutive terms tend to infinity?
justification: The draft is the exact open problem stated in the paper as Pillai's conjecture. In Section 1.2, after recalling Catalan's theorem for the special case k = 1, Waldschmidt writes: 'Let k be a positive integer. The equation x^p - y^q = k, where the unknowns x, y, p and q take integer values, all >= 2, has only finitely many solutions (x, y, p, q).' He immediately adds the equivalent reformulation about gaps between consecutive perfect powers, and then notes that even the case k = 2 is unknown and mentions the related question x^p - y^q = 6. The stronger neighboring Shorey conjecture is presented only afterward as implying Pillai's, so the narrow paper-faithful target is Conjecture 1.3 itself rather than that broader polynomial variant.

original_question: Let K be a number field with a real embedding, let V be a smooth variety over K, and let Z be the real-topological closure of V(K) inside V(R). When K = Q and V(Q) is Zariski dense, must Z be a union of connected components of V(R)?

correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official formulation very closely. refined_question: Let K be a number field equipped with a real embedding, let V be a smooth variety over K, and let Z be the closure of V(K) in V(R) for the real topology. Assume that K = Q and that V(Q) is Zariski dense in V. Is Z necessarily a union of connected components of V(R)?

original_question: For n >= 2, describe the set of real numbers xi such that there are constants c_1(xi), c_2(xi) > 0 with uniform lower bounds for approximation by algebraic numbers of degree at most n, while infinitely many algebraic numbers of degree exactly n achieve the corresponding Dirichlet-type upper bound.

correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the main ingredients of the target statement: an integer n >= 2, a set of real numbers xi, constants c_1(xi), c_2(xi) > 0 depending on xi, a uniform lower bound for approximation by algebraic numbers of bounded degree, and the existence of infinitely many algebraic approximants satisfying a matching upper bound at the same exponent scale.

refined_question: For an integer n >= 2, let A_n be the set of real numbers xi such that there exist constants c_1(xi), c_2(xi) > 0 with the following properties: for every algebraic number alpha with [Q(alpha):Q] <= n, one has |xi - alpha| >= c_2(xi) H(alpha)^(-(n+1)); and there exist infinitely many algebraic numbers alpha with [Q(alpha):Q] <= n such that |xi - alpha| <= c_1(xi) H(alpha)^(-(n+1)), where H(alpha) denotes the usual height of the minimal polynomial of alpha over Z. justification: The draft is aiming at the narrow metric question officially stated as Question 5.2, not at the broader metrical sets F_kappa and F'_kappa and not merely at the upper-bound statement of the Wirsing-Schmidt conjecture. original_question: Let (n_i) be an increasing sequence of positive integers, and suppose there is a prime p such that the power series sum z^{n_i} in F_p[[z]] is algebraic over F_p(z). Must the real number sum 10^{-n_i} be either rational or transcendental?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 5.4 (Loxton and van der Poorten) in §5.2, "Function Fields".
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the main objects and arithmetic direction of the paper's statement: an increasing sequence of positive integers, the existence of a prime p, the lacunary formal power series f(z) = ∑_{i>=0} z^{n_i} viewed in F_p[[z]], the hypothesis that f is algebraic over F_p(z), and the transcendence question for the associated real number α = ∑_{i>=0} 10^{-n_i}.
missing_details: ["The paper states the sequence as (n_i)_{i>=0} and writes both sums explicitly over i>=0.", "A crucial hypothesis is missing: the formal power series f(z) = ∑_{i>=0} z^{n_i} must be irrational in the function-field sense, namely f(z) not in F_p(z).", "The parenthetical clarification 'irrational (i.e., does not belong to F_p(z))' refers to the formal power series, not to the real number α.", "The paper does not ask for the weaker dichotomy 'rational or transcendental'; it asks directly whether α is transcendental under the added hypothesis f(z) not in F_p(z).", "The statement belongs specifically to the function-field / automata-theory context of §5.2, so the refined question should keep that scope rather than recast it as a broader decimal-expansion problem."]
refined_question: Let (n_i)_{i>=0} be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers. Suppose there exists a prime number p such that the formal power series f(z) = ∑_{i>=0} z^{n_i} in F_p[[z]] is algebraic over F_p(z) and irrational in the sense that f(z) does not belong to F_p(z). Must the real number α = ∑_{i>=0} 10^{-n_i} be transcendental?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: let (n_i)_{i>=0} be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers, and assume that for some prime p the series f(z) = ∑_{i>=0} z^{n_i} lies in F_p[[z]], is algebraic over F_p(z), and satisfies f(z) not in F_p(z). Is the real number ∑_{i>=0} 10^{-n_i} transcendental?
justification: This draft is clearly targeting Conjecture 5.4, because the paper's statement uses exactly the same ingredients: an increasing sequence (n_i), a prime p, the series ∑ z^{n_i} in F_p[[z]], algebraicity over F_p(z), and the decimal number ∑ 10^{-n_i}. In §5.2 Waldschmidt introduces the conjecture as part of the function-field and automata-theoretic transcendence discussion, then states it with one extra hypothesis that your draft omits: the formal series must be 'irrational,' explicitly glossed as 'does not belong to F_p(z)'. Under that hypothesis, the paper asks for transcendence of the real number itself, not merely whether it is 'rational or transcendental.' So your draft is close to the intended target, but it is not fully paper-faithful until that nonrationality hypothesis is restored and the conclusion is sharpened back to pure transcendence.

original_question: What additional invariants, recognition methods, or classification principles can distinguish the Kishino virtual knot from the unknot and clarify when a non-trivial virtual knot can arise as the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots, especially in view of the fact that connected sum is not well defined for closed virtual knots but is ordered and well defined for long virtual knots?
target_in_paper: Section 7, Problem 1, "Recognising the Kishino Knot."
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the paper’s main target: the Kishino knot as a paradigmatic nontrivial virtual knot that can arise as a connected sum of two trivial virtual knot diagrams, together with the key distinction that connected sum is not well defined for closed/compact virtual knots but is ordered and well defined in the long-virtual-knot category. It also correctly keeps the focus on recognition/distinguishing methods and on the related classification issue rather than drifting to broader virtual-knot problems.
missing_details: ["The nearest official formulation is Section 7, Problem 1, explicitly titled \"Recognising the Kishino Knot,\" so the target is not a general search for stronger virtual-knot invariants but this specific Kishino/connected-sum problem.", "The paper records five already known ways to detect Kishino’s nontriviality: the 3-strand Jones polynomial, the Ξ-polynomial, the quaternionic biquandle, the surface bracket polynomial, and Kadokami’s proof via the immersion class of a shadow curve in genus two.", "The paper phrases the first part as: even though Kishino is already recognized by several methods, \"other proofs of its non-triviality may be illuminating\"; your draft should reflect that this is about further illuminating recognitions/proofs, not a broader classification of all possible invariants.", "The second part is specifically: classify when a nontrivial virtual knot can be the connected sum of two trivial virtual knots.", "The hidden reason for that classification problem is that connected sum of closed/compact virtual knots is not well defined, so different choices of connected-sum operation can produce genuinely different effects.", "The paper adds one more closely related target that your draft only hints at: classify the different long virtual knots whose closures are equivalent to the unknot.", "No ambient ring, coefficient field, polynomial variables, homogeneity conditions, degree restrictions, or nilpotency hypotheses belong to this problem; it is a categorical/classificatory virtual-knot problem rather than an algebraic one."]
refined_question: Given that the Kishino virtual knot is already known to be nontrivial by the 3-strand Jones polynomial, the Ξ-polynomial, the quaternionic biquandle, the surface bracket polynomial, and Kadokami’s genus-two shadow-curve method, can one find further illuminating recognitions/proofs of its nontriviality and, more fundamentally, classify exactly when a nontrivial compact virtual knot can occur as a connected sum of two trivial virtual knots, taking into account that connected sum for closed virtual knots is not well defined, whereas for long virtual knots it is an ordered well-defined operation; closely relatedly, can one classify the long virtual knots whose closures are equivalent to the unknot?
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper’s Section 7, Problem 1, not at a neighboring problem. That problem explicitly starts from known ways of recognizing Kishino, asks whether further proofs would still be illuminating, and then sharpens the issue to the classification of nontrivial virtual knots that arise as connected sums of two trivial virtual knots. The surrounding Section 2 discussion supplies the essential hidden assumptions: closed/compact virtual connected sum is not well defined, long connected sum is well defined but ordered, and Kishino is the motivating example coming from two long pieces. Section 3.3 gives the nearby technical context that Kishino defeats some standard Alexander-biquandle-style detectors while being detected by other methods, which explains why the paper singles it out.

original_question: Can new combinatorial invariants be constructed for flat virtual knots and links, and can the structure of the flat biquandle algebra be better understood despite the fact that it is isomorphic to the Weyl algebra and has no non-trivial finite-dimensional representations?
target_in_paper: Section 7, Problem 2 ("Flat Virtuals").
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the two core components of the paper's official open problem: (i) finding new combinatorial invariants for flat virtual knots and links, and (ii) understanding the flat biquandle algebra, with the paper explicitly noting that this algebra is isomorphic to the Weyl algebra and has no non-trivial finite-dimensional representations. It also keeps the discussion focused on flat virtual objects rather than drifting to broader questions about virtual knots in general.

refined_question: For flat virtual knots and links (also called virtual strings), defined as diagrams with virtual crossings and undecorated flat crossings modulo generalized flat Reidemeister moves, can one construct new combinatorial invariants of flat virtuals and clarify the structure of the flat biquandle algebra, which the paper notes is isomorphic to the Weyl algebra and has no non-trivial finite-dimensional representations, in particular with the aim of obtaining invariants that detect flat linking phenomena beyond the mod 2 linking number?
justification: The draft is aiming at exactly Section 7, Problem 2, not a broader neighboring problem. The official formulation there is: flat virtual knots and links are difficult to classify; one should find new combinatorial invariants of flat virtuals, and one would like to know more about the flat biquandle algebra, with the added remarks that it is isomorphic to the Weyl algebra, has no non-trivial finite-dimensional representations, and that only small examples are known which detect some flat linking beyond mod 2 linking numbers (Section 7, Problem 2, p. 21). Section 2.1 provides the stand-alone context needed to sharpen the question: it defines flat virtual diagrams, their equivalence via generalized flat Reidemeister moves, and explains that few invariants were known and that irreducibility of the underlying flat diagram is a first obstruction to classicality (Section 2.1, pp. 3-4). I therefore kept the rewrite narrowly on flat virtuals/virtual strings and did not broaden it to other biquandle, virtual braid, or general virtual-knot problems.

original_question: Give an example of a smooth projective curve X over a field of characteristic p > 0 together with a finite group action rho: G -> Aut(X) such that, for the deformation hull R(X, rho), the characteristic nu(X, rho) equals p^n for some finite n > 1.
target_in_paper: Section 3, Problem 3.1, in Gunther Cornelissen's contribution "Lifting an automorphism group to finite characteristic".
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the precise problem in the paper: it asks for an example, not a classification; it uses the paper's notation R(X, rho) and nu(X, rho); it places X in characteristic p > 0; and it asks for the specific intermediate finite characteristic phenomenon nu(X, rho) = p^n with n > 1 finite.

refined_question: Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0, let X/k be a smooth projective curve, and let rho: G -> Aut_k(X) be an action of a finite group G on X. Let W(k) be the ring of Witt vectors of k, let C be the category of local Artinian W(k)-algebras with residue field k, and let D(X, rho) be the deformation functor sending A in C to the set of isomorphism classes of liftings of (X, rho) to A, where a lifting means a smooth finite-type A-scheme X' with special fiber X together with a G-action G -> Aut_A(X') lifting rho. Let R(X, rho) be the Schlessinger prorepresentable hull of D(X, rho), and define nu(X, rho) := char(R(X, rho)). Give an example of a group action (X, rho) such that nu(X, rho) = p^n for some finite integer n > 1.
equivalent_formulation: When H^0(X, T_X)^G = 0 (for instance if g(X) >= 2), so that R(X, rho) prorepresents D(X, rho), one can equivalently ask for an action (X, rho) such that nu(X, rho) = sup{char(A) : A in L(X, rho)} = p^n for some finite n > 1, where L(X, rho) = {A in C : there exists a lift of (X, rho) to A}, with the convention that the supremum of an unbounded chain p, p^2, p^3, ... is 0.
justification: The draft is targeting Section 3 rather than the paper's earlier conjectural material, because the notation R(X, rho) and nu(X, rho) is introduced exactly in Cornelissen's short note on lifting automorphism groups. The official problem is Problem 3.1, whose statement is essentially the same existential question as the draft. To make it stand alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the surrounding definitions from the opening paragraphs of Section 3: the Witt-vector base W(k), the Artinian category C, the deformation functor D(X, rho), the meaning of a lift, and the definition of nu(X, rho) as the characteristic of the hull. Remark 3.2 supplies an important nearby restriction: weakly ramified actions cannot yield examples with finite exponent n > 1. Remark 3.6 gives the paper's explicit reformulation of nu(X, rho) in terms of the supremum of the characteristics of Artinian lift rings when prorepresentability holds.

original_question: Let X be a topological space. target_in_paper: Problem 9.2 in §9, Function spaces and local-global principles: Is S1(Γ0,Γ0) for Cp(X) equivalent to S1(Γ,Γ) for X? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s target almost verbatim: it asks about a set of reals X, the property S1(Γ0,Γ0) of Cp(X), and whether that is equivalent to S1(Γ,Γ) of X. That is exactly the official Problem 9.2 in §9. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))

([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))", "The point 0 must be identified as the constant zero function in Cp(X). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))", "Γ0 needs to be unpacked via the local definition from §9: Γ0 is the family of countably infinite subsets A of Cp(X) such that 0 = lim A, i.e. 0 is not in A and every neighborhood of 0 contains all but finitely many elements of A. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))", "S1(A,B) should be stated explicitly: for each sequence (Un)n∈ℕ of members of A, one can choose Un∈Un for each n so that {Un:n∈ℕ} is a member of B. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))", "Γ should be defined as the family of open γ-covers of X, where a γ-cover is an infinite open cover U of X such that each x∈X belongs to all but finitely many members of U; the paper also adopts the convention that a cover is nontrivial, meaning X itself is not an element of the cover. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))", "To reflect the paper’s exact intent, it helps to note the known one-way implication stated immediately before the problem: S1(Γ,Γ) for X implies S1(Γ0,Γ0) for Cp(X), so the open issue is the converse. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))"]
refined_question: Let X⊆ℝ∖ℚ, let Cp(X) be the space of all continuous real-valued functions on X with the topology of pointwise convergence, and let 0 denote the constant zero function. For collections A,B, write S1(A,B) to mean that for every sequence (Un)n∈ℕ of members of A, there exist Un∈Un for each n such that {Un:n∈ℕ} is a member of B. Let Γ0 be the family of countably infinite subsets A⊆Cp(X) with 0=lim A (equivalently, 0∉A and every neighborhood of 0 contains all but finitely many points of A), and let Γ be the family of open γ-covers of X, where a γ-cover is an infinite nontrivial open cover U of X such that each x∈X belongs to all but finitely many members of U. Since S1(Γ,Γ) for X is known to imply S1(Γ0,Γ0) for Cp(X), does the converse hold? Equivalently, is S1(Γ0,Γ0) for Cp(X) equivalent to S1(Γ,Γ) for X? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))
equivalent_formulation: The paper states that S1(Γ0,Γ0) for Cp(X) is equivalent to S1(CΓ,CΓ) for X, where CΓ denotes the family of clopen γ-covers of X; therefore Problem 9.2 reduces to asking whether S1(Γ,Γ)=S1(CΓ,CΓ) for X. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))
justification: The draft clearly targets §9 rather than any earlier problem: the wording is essentially the same as Problem 9.2. To make it fully stand-alone and faithful to the paper, one must import the §1 definitions of S1 and γ-covers, the §9 local notation Γx at the point 0, the definition of Cp(X), and the hidden standing assumption X⊆ℝ∖ℚ. I also preserved the paper’s immediate contextual framing that one implication is already known and the open content is the converse. The alternate formulation is included only because the paper itself explicitly states the equivalence with S1(CΓ,CΓ). ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0609601))

original_question: Let K be the Kasteleyn matrix of an a, b, c semiregular hexagon, and let the associated Carlitz matrix be the b-by-b matrix obtained from K by row and column reductions, with entries given by binomial coefficients. Determine the cokernel of these Carlitz matrices, equivalently the cokernel of the Kasteleyn matrices of a, b, c hexagons, and if possible interpret that cokernel in terms of lozenge tilings.
target_in_paper: Section 2 ("Lozenges"), Problem 5: determine the cokernel of the Carlitz matrix, equivalently of the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the a,b,c semiregular hexagon, and if possible interpret that cokernel in terms of the tilings.

refined_question: For positive integers a,b,c, let H(a,b,c) be the semiregular hexagon with side lengths a,b,c,a,b,c, and let K_{a,b,c} be the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the finite honeycomb graph dual to H(a,b,c) (equivalently here, the ordinary bipartite adjacency matrix). Let C_{a,b,c} be the integer b-by-b Carlitz matrix obtained from K_{a,b,c} by integral row and column reductions, with (i,j)-entry C_{ij} = (a+c choose a+i-j). Determine the finite abelian group coker_Z(C_{a,b,c}) = Z^b / im(C_{a,b,c}) — equivalently coker_Z(K_{a,b,c}), and hence the common cokernel of the three Carlitz matrices arising from permuting a,b,c — and, if possible, give a direct interpretation of this cokernel in terms of lozenge tilings (equivalently matchings) of H(a,b,c).
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: determine, over Z, the cokernel of the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix of the finite honeycomb graph dual to the a,b,c semiregular hexagon, and if possible interpret that group in terms of the lozenge tilings of the hexagon.
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of the paper’s Section 2, Problem 5. The nearby setup first defines the a,b,c semiregular hexagon and identifies its lozenge tilings with matchings of the dual honeycomb graph. It then states that systematic row and column reduction of the Kasteleyn-Percus matrix yields the b-by-b Carlitz matrix with entries (a+c choose a+i-j), and explicitly says that these reductions do not change the cokernel, understood as an abelian group whose order is the determinant. The same paragraph adds the permutation symmetry in a,b,c, producing three nontrivially different Carlitz matrices with the same cokernel. The official problem statement is therefore exactly the cokernel-determination problem together with the optional request for a tiling interpretation; it is not a broader question about arbitrary planar graphs or about other matrix invariants. The examples c=1 (cyclic cokernel) and a=b=c=2 (noncyclic cokernel Z/2Z x Z/10Z) are contextual motivation, not part of the formal statement.

refined_question: Let Ω ⊂ ℂ^n be a bounded strongly pseudoconvex domain, let k_Ω denote its Kobayashi distance, and let ρ_Δ denote the Poincaré distance on the unit disc Δ. Does there exist an integer K = K(Ω) such that for every pair of points p, q ∈ Ω there are holomorphic maps f_1, ..., f_N : Δ → Ω with N ≤ K and points a_j, b_j ∈ Δ satisfying f_1(a_1) = p, f_j(b_j) = f_{j+1}(a_{j+1}) for 1 ≤ j < N, f_N(b_N) = q, and k_Ω(p, q) = Σ_{j=1}^N ρ_Δ(a_j, b_j)? Equivalently, is the minimal length of a Kobayashi chain realizing the distance between p and q uniformly bounded over all p, q ∈ Ω?
justification: The draft is already close to the intended problem, but it leaves several definitions implicit and uses the potentially misleading phrase 'absolute constant'. The closest precise formulation recoverable from the original item and its later quotation is a uniform bound on the length of a distance-realizing chain of holomorphic discs, depending only on the strongly pseudoconvex domain and not on the endpoints. A later paper by Myung-Yull Pang explicitly attributes to Krantz the conjecture that for a strongly pseudoconvex domain there is a fixed constant K = K(D) such that the Kobayashi distance between any two points is realized by a chain of holomorphic maps of length less than K; Pang also explains that convex domains have the extremal case K = 1. That quotation aligns with your draft's mathematical target, while making clear the need to define the chain and the realization equality.
